name: A. A. Dun
bio: The British poet and psychogeographer Aidan Andrew Dun, who publishes under his full name. A grandson of the dancer Marie Rambert, he spent his childhood in the West Indies, returned to London as a teenager to live with her, and left school without qualifications before some years of travelling. Twenty-three years in the writing, his first epic, Vale Royal (1995), a quest in terza rima through the buried mythology of King's Cross, was launched at the Royal Albert Hall and earned him the title 'Voice of King's Cross'. Further verse epics followed, among them Universal (2002), The Uninhabitable City (2005) and the sonnet-novel McCool (2010).

bio: The name under which the American author and speaker Esther Hicks presents what she describes as inspired teachings, delivered as messages from a non-physical group intelligence she calls 'Abraham'. With her late husband Jerry she built these into a highly successful series of workshops and books, among them Ask and It Is Given, that became a cornerstone of the modern law-of-attraction movement. The teachings hold that our thoughts and feelings shape our reality, and that aligning with positive emotion draws well-being toward us.

name: Abraham Lincoln
bio: The sixteenth president of the United States, who held the nation together through its civil war and ended slavery within it. Born in a Kentucky log cabin and almost entirely self-taught, he rose through frontier Illinois as a lawyer and politician, opposing the spread of slavery with homely eloquence. Elected in 1860, he watched the southern states secede and led the Union through four years of terrible war, issuing the Emancipation Proclamation and, at Gettysburg, restating the country's founding promise of equality. Five days after Lee's surrender at Appomattox, and six weeks into the second term he had won the previous November, he was shot in a Washington theatre.

name: Abraham Maslow
bio: An American psychologist who helped found humanistic psychology, a 'third force' beyond behaviourism and psychoanalysis focused on health and human potential rather than illness. The eldest child of poor Jewish immigrants in Brooklyn, he studied our higher motivations and coined the idea of a hierarchy of needs, often drawn as a pyramid rising from food and safety through love and esteem to 'self-actualisation', the full realisation of one's gifts. Later he wrote of peak experiences and of a psychology reaching beyond the self, shaping counselling, education, management and the human-potential movement.

name: Alan Watts
bio: A British-born philosopher and writer who became one of the great popularisers of Eastern thought in the West. Fascinated by Buddhism as a schoolboy in England, he moved to the United States and left the Episcopal priesthood to interpret Zen, Taoism and Hindu philosophy for a wide audience. Through more than twenty books, among them The Way of Zen and The Wisdom of Insecurity, and a stream of witty, spellbinding lectures, he taught that the self is not a separate ego but one with the flowing universe. A charismatic, hard-living sage, he became a guru of the 1960s counterculture.

name: Albert Camus
bio: A French-Algerian writer and philosopher, one of the great moral voices of the twentieth century. Born poor in French Algeria and raised by a nearly silent, illiterate mother, he became a novelist, playwright, journalist and wartime Resistance editor. His novels The Stranger and The Plague and the essays The Myth of Sisyphus and The Rebel explore the 'absurd', the clash between our hunger for meaning and a silent universe, and answer it not with despair but with lucid revolt, solidarity and love of life. He won the Nobel Prize in 1957 and, two years later, at forty-six, died in a car crash.

name: Albert Einstein
bio: A German-born theoretical physicist whose work remade our picture of reality. In 1905, his 'miracle year', while working as a Swiss patent clerk, he published papers on the light quantum, on Brownian motion and on special relativity, uniting space and time and giving the equation E=mc2. A decade later his general theory of relativity recast gravity as the curving of spacetime, confirmed when starlight was seen to bend around the sun. He won the Nobel Prize in 1921 and, a Jew and a pacifist, fled Nazi Germany for Princeton, where he lived out his last decades and warned against the atomic weapons his physics had made possible.

name: Albert Schweitzer
bio: An Alsatian polymath who gave up brilliant European careers to become a jungle doctor in Africa. Already renowned as a theologian, philosopher and organist and a leading interpreter of Bach, he trained in his thirties as a physician and in 1913 founded a hospital at Lambarene in what is now Gabon, where he served for most of the rest of his life. His ethic of 'reverence for life', a boundless responsibility toward every living thing, won him the Nobel Peace Prize in 1952, which he used to speak out against nuclear weapons. Revered in his day as a living saint, he remains a symbol of self-sacrifice.

name: Alexis Carrel
bio: A French surgeon and biologist whose brilliance was later shadowed by his politics. Working in the United States, he pioneered techniques for sewing blood vessels together and for keeping tissues and organs alive outside the body, advances that made modern vascular and transplant surgery possible and won him the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1912. His hugely popular book Man, the Unknown, however, called for the renewal of humankind through eugenics, in terms that anticipated Nazi thinking, and his reputation fell sharply after his death for his role under the Vichy regime.

name: Alfred A. Montapert
bio: An American businessman who became a prolific author of popular self-improvement books built around aphorisms and 'laws of life'. Four decades in business, most of them in Los Angeles, lay behind the anthology Distilled Wisdom (1964), a planning manual for executives (1967) and, above all, The Supreme Philosophy of Man: The Laws of Life (Prentice-Hall, 1970), which was reprinted for decades and translated into French. Words of Wisdom to Live By (1986) gathered his own maxims on work, health and happiness, short and emphatic lines that still circulate widely, though little was publicly recorded of his private life.

bio: A contemporary American writer, speaker and self-love advocate who grew up in Fort Collins, Colorado, and lives there still. Drawing on her own recovery from an abusive relationship and years of disordered eating, she published Bad Fat Person (2019), part memoir and part social commentary on body image, fatness and unconditional self-regard, and has written essays for the Huffington Post and other outlets. bio: A French-born writer of Cuban and Danish descent, known above all for the diaries she kept from the age of eleven until her death, published from 1966 onward. She lived in Paris in the 1930s, where she was close to Henry Miller, and later in New York and Los Angeles. Her other work includes the novels collected as Cities of the Interior and the erotica published as Delta of Venus (1977).

His works include The Crime of Sylvestre Bonnard (1881), Thaïs (1890) and The Gods Are Athirst (1912), written in a clear, ironic and sceptical style. Trained in journalism and mass communication, with an MFA in creative writing and a holistic health coach's certificate, she went on to build the platforms Creative Rehab, Write Yourself Alive and the Self-Creation School, to help people heal and remake their lives through writing and other art. name: Anne Lamott
bio: An American novelist and essayist beloved for her honest, funny and generous writing on faith, addiction, motherhood and the writing life. Raised in the San Francisco Bay Area, she drew on her own struggles with alcoholism, single parenthood and belief in books that mix confession, comedy and grace. Her guide to writing, Bird by Bird, with its counsel to take hard things 'bird by bird', has become a classic of the craft, and Traveling Mercies and other memoirs made her a distinctive Christian voice: unorthodox, progressive and self-deprecating. She is also a longtime teacher and popular speaker.

name: Annie Dillard
bio: An American author who won the Pulitzer Prize at twenty-nine for Pilgrim at Tinker Creek, a rapt, searching book of observations of the natural world near her Virginia home. Trained in theology and writing, she brings a mystic's intensity and a naturalist's precision to questions of beauty, cruelty, God and mortality. Across essays, poetry, memoir and the novel The Living, she treats seeing clearly and paying attention as almost a spiritual discipline. Her slender, dense meditation The Writing Life and books such as Holy the Firm are prized for their sentence-by-sentence brilliance.

name: Anthony Burgess
bio: A prodigiously versatile English writer and composer, best known for the dystopian novel A Clockwork Orange. Raised Catholic in Manchester and long a schoolteacher, including in colonial Malaya, he published his first novel at thirty-nine and had almost finished his Malayan trilogy when, late in 1959, he collapsed in a Brunei classroom and was told, wrongly, that a brain tumour left him a year to live; he then wrote at a furious pace to provide for his wife. His novel of a violent youth and a chilling state 'cure', with its invented Russian-tinged slang, became a byword for debates about free will and violence. He also composed music, reviewed voraciously and produced dozens of erudite, playful and linguistically dazzling books.

bio: A French aviator and writer who turned the perilous early years of flight into literature. Carrying mail over the Pyrenees, the Sahara and the Andes for the pioneering Aeropostale, he drew on that life in lyrical books such as Night Flight and Wind, Sand and Stars, meditations on danger, courage and human solidarity. Exiled in New York during the Second World War, he wrote and illustrated The Little Prince, a deceptively simple fable that became one of the most translated books ever written. He then returned to fly reconnaissance for the Free French and vanished over the Mediterranean in the summer of 1944.

name: Antonio Machado
bio: One of Spain's greatest modern poets and a leading voice of the Generation of '98. Born in Seville and raised in Madrid, he taught French for a living and spent formative years in the old Castilian town of Soria, whose stark landscape and the early death of his young wife haunt his spare, meditative verse. Collections such as Solitudes and Fields of Castile turn plain words, roads, rivers and the passing of time into a quiet philosophy. A committed republican, he left Barcelona as Franco's troops closed in and crossed the French border in the last days of January 1939, reaching the coastal village of Collioure ill and exhausted; he died there less than a month later, three days before his mother.

name: Aristotle
bio: A Greek philosopher and polymath whose range and influence are almost without parallel. Born at Stagira in the north, he studied for twenty years under Plato at the Academy in Athens, then tutored the young Alexander the Great, and later founded his own school, the Lyceum. He wrote on nearly everything: logic, which he all but invented, physics, biology, metaphysics, ethics, politics, rhetoric and poetics. His insistence on observation and system, and his ideas of virtue as a mean and of the good life as flourishing, shaped medieval Christian, Jewish and Islamic thought and still underpin much of Western science and philosophy.

There, in 1970, she launched The Love Project, an experiment in transforming a troubled school through unconditional love, and formulated a set of 'Love Principles', among them 'Be the change you want to see', a line often later credited to Gandhi. She has since written more than a dozen books and co-directs the Teleos Institute in Arizona.

name: Arthur Ashe
bio: An American tennis champion and humanitarian, the first Black man to win the US Open, the Australian Open and Wimbledon. Raised under segregation in Richmond, Virginia, he rose to the top of a nearly all-white sport, then used his fame for larger causes, campaigning against apartheid and for education and health. Forced to retire by heart disease, he contracted HIV from a blood transfusion and, once his illness became public, spent his final months as an eloquent advocate for AIDS awareness. He died at forty-nine, remembered for his character as much as his game.

name: Arthur Rubinstein

A prodigy from Lodz who first played in public as a small boy, he went on to a career of more than eight decades, admired above all for his Chopin, which combined warmth, colour and aristocratic ease. After a wayward, pleasure-loving youth he rededicated himself to his art in middle age and reached new heights. Famously charming, cultured and full of life, he went on giving recitals into his late eighties, and championed Spanish and modern music alongside the Romantic repertoire he loved.

bio: An Indian yoga master who did more than almost anyone to spread the practice of yoga around the world. Born into poverty in Karnataka and sickly as a child, he took up yoga to strengthen his frail body, then developed a rigorous, precise method that emphasises exact bodily alignment and the long holding of postures, often with the aid of props he devised. His book Light on Yoga became an international classic, and the institute he built in Pune drew students from everywhere. Through the discipline that bears his name, Iyengar Yoga, he helped turn an ancient spiritual practice into a global phenomenon.

name: Benjamin Disraeli
bio: A British statesman and novelist who twice served as prime minister and did much to shape modern Conservatism. Of Italian-Jewish descent and baptised a Christian as a boy, he overcame prejudice and early debts to rise through Parliament by wit, ambition and dazzling oratory. As Lord Derby's chancellor he carried the Reform Act of 1867, which roughly doubled the electorate; as prime minister he pursued an assertive imperial policy and made Queen Victoria, who came to prefer him to any of her ministers, Empress of India. A glittering rival to Gladstone, he was also a successful novelist, whose books such as Sybil dramatised the gulf between rich and poor, 'the two nations', in Victorian Britain.

name: Bernard Baruch
bio: An American financier and statesman who became known as an elder adviser to presidents. The son of a South Carolina doctor, he made a great fortune speculating on Wall Street before he was thirty, then turned to public service, mobilising American industry in the First World War as chairman of the War Industries Board and advising presidents from Wilson to Truman, for whom he put the 1946 Baruch Plan for international control of atomic energy to the United Nations. Fond of thinking in the open air, he was nicknamed the 'park bench statesman'. Shrewd, independent and endlessly quotable, he dispensed plain-spoken wisdom on money, politics and human nature well into a long old age.

bio: An American singer, guitarist and songwriter, the co-founder and frontman of the punk-rock band Green Day. Raised in the working-class town of Rodeo, near the San Francisco Bay, he formed the band with a schoolfriend as a teenager, and their 1994 album Dookie carried a new wave of pop-punk into the mainstream. A decade later the ambitious rock opera American Idiot, a jaundiced portrait of Bush-era America, revived the band and even reached Broadway. Restless and prolific, Armstrong has written some of the most widely sung anthems of his generation while keeping a punk's suspicion of authority.

name: Blaise Pascal
bio: A French mathematician, physicist and religious thinker of dazzling gifts who died at thirty-nine. A child prodigy, he founded the theory of probability with Fermat, built one of the first mechanical calculators, and proved fundamental results about air pressure and the vacuum. A profound religious experience drew him toward the austere Catholicism of Port-Royal, which he defended in the witty Provincial Letters. His unfinished notes toward a defence of Christianity, published after his death as the Pensees, contain some of the most searching writing ever set down on faith, doubt and the contradictions of the human condition.

name: Buckminster Fuller
bio: An American architect, inventor, designer and futurist who preached doing 'more with less' for all humanity. After early failure and despair, he resolved to devote his life to serving the world through what he called design science. He is best known for the geodesic dome, the light, strong, sphere-like structure that became his signature, and for popularising 'Spaceship Earth', the phrase his Operating Manual for Spaceship Earth carried to a wide public. Restlessly inventive, he coined 'tensegrity' and 'synergetics', produced the Dymaxion car and house, striking world maps and bold schemes for housing and energy, and travelled the globe lecturing tirelessly on how technology might let everyone thrive on a finite planet.

After years of searching he is said to have awakened under a fig tree at Bodh Gaya, and for the next forty-five years he taught across the plains of the Ganges a middle way between indulgence and self-denial, setting out the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path that lead beyond suffering.

name: Cardinal de Retz (Jean François Paul de Gondi)
bio: A French cardinal, political intriguer and one of the great memoirists in the language. Born Jean Francois Paul de Gondi, he was pushed into the church against his restless, ambitious nature, and became a leading agitator in the Fronde, the mid-century revolt of nobles and the parlement against the crown and Cardinal Mazarin. Imprisoned and then exiled after its failure, he spent his last years writing Memoirs of extraordinary vividness and psychological insight, painting the personalities and manoeuvres of his age with a cynical, penetrating eye. They rank among the finest French prose of the seventeenth century.

name: Carl Jung
bio: A Swiss psychiatrist who founded analytical psychology. An early collaborator of Freud, he broke with him over the nature of the unconscious, which Jung saw as far more than a store of repressed desire. He proposed a deeper 'collective unconscious' shared by all humanity and peopled by archetypes, primordial images such as the shadow, the anima and the self that surface in dreams, myth and religion. He brought the terms introvert and extravert into psychology, defining them as the directions in which psychic energy flows, explored alchemy, astrology and Eastern thought, and understood life as a lifelong process of individuation, the gradual integration of the psyche toward wholeness.
notes: Jung introduced introversion and extraversion as psychological types, first in a 1909 Clark University lecture and systematically in Psychologische Typen (1921), but he did not coin the words, which had earlier currency in European thought.

name: Carl Sandburg
bio: An American poet, biographer and folk-song collector, a bard of the industrial Midwest and its working people. The son of Swedish immigrants in Illinois, he left school early, rode the rails and worked many jobs before finding his voice in free verse of plain, muscular American speech, hailing Chicago as the 'City of the Big Shoulders'. He won Pulitzer Prizes both for his poetry and for his monumental life of Abraham Lincoln, and toured the country reciting his verse and singing the folk songs he had gathered. Warm, rumpled and democratic, he became one of the best-loved literary figures of his day.

name: Caroline Myss
bio: An American author and speaker on spirituality, consciousness and healing, who describes herself as a 'medical intuitive', claiming to sense the energetic and emotional roots of physical illness. Trained in journalism and then theology, she co-founded the publisher Stillpoint in New Hampshire and worked with the physician C. Norman Shealy before her own books made her famous: Anatomy of the Spirit (1996), which links the body's energy centres to psychology and spirit, and, in the next decade, Sacred Contracts. A dynamic lecturer, she teaches that our biography becomes our biology and that healing is bound up with forgiveness, power and meaning. She has a wide following, though her ideas are viewed sceptically by mainstream medicine.
notes: Born 2 December 1952 in Chicago. Sacred Contracts belongs to the 2000s, so the bio no longer counts it among the 1990s books that made her name; her degrees are a journalism BA (1974) and a theology MA (1979).
checked: myss.com press biography (her own site); Wikipedia; Encyclopedia.com (Contemporary Authors entry on Myss)

name: Cato the Elder
bio: A Roman senator, soldier and writer, the very model of old-fashioned Roman severity. A self-made man from the farming class, he rose to the highest offices, campaigned in Spain and Greece, and as censor policed public morals with famous strictness, taxing luxury and purging the Senate. Suspicious of Greek refinement and of Rome's great rival, he is said to have ended every speech, whatever its subject, with the demand that Carthage be destroyed. He also composed the first history of Rome written in Latin and a blunt, practical manual on running a farm.
notes: Cato the Elder, or the Censor, to distinguish him from his great-grandson. Deathplace emptied: he died in 149 BC but no ancient source records where. Plutarch has news reaching him at Rome shortly before the end, and 'Rome' was an inference from that.
checked: Britannica; Wikipedia; Plutarch, Life of Cato the Elder ch. 27 (Perseus and the Loeb text via Bill Thayer's Penelope)

name: Charles Baudelaire
bio: A French poet and critic who stands at the threshold of modern poetry. A dandy and spendthrift in bohemian Paris, he distilled the beauty and squalor of the modern city into Les Fleurs du mal, a book so frank about sex, decay and despair that he and his publisher were prosecuted for offending public morals. He wrote of the artificial and the fleeting, gave the idea of 'modernity' its meaning, and championed Wagner and Delacroix as a pioneering critic. His prose poems and his translations of Edgar Allan Poe were as influential as his verse. Ill and impoverished, he died at forty-six, his true reputation still to come.
checked: Wikipedia; Encyclopedia.com (Baudelaire); The Art Story chronology of the 1857 prosecution and the Poe translations

name: Charles Bukowski
bio: A German-born American writer who became the laureate of skid row. Brought to Los Angeles as a small child, he endured a violent father and disfiguring acne, then passed decades in low-paying jobs, rented rooms and bars, publishing little until his forties. Taken up by the small press Black Sparrow, he poured out poems, stories and novels in a plain, hard-bitten voice, most of it filtered through his drinking, womanising alter ego Henry Chinaski. Books such as Post Office and Ham on Rye made him an unlikely cult hero, prized for honesty, endurance and the battered dignity of the down-and-out.
notes: Died at San Pedro Peninsula Hospital in San Pedro, the Los Angeles port district where he lived, rather than in Los Angeles at large; he is buried at Green Hills Memorial Park, Rancho Palos Verdes. Sounes dates the family's move from Baltimore to Los Angeles to 1924, when he was three.
checked: New York Times obituary, 11 March 1994; UPI, 10 March 1994; Howard Sounes, Charles Bukowski: Locked in the Arms of a Crazy Life (extract on the publisher's site); Wikipedia

name: Charles Goodhart
bio: A British economist and central bank adviser best known for the principle that bears his name. He spent seventeen years at the Bank of England, becoming a chief adviser in 1980, then held the chair of banking and finance at the London School of Economics and sat on the Bank's first Monetary Policy Committee from 1997 to 2000. In a 1975 paper he observed that once a measure of the economy is made a target of policy, people adjust their behaviour and it stops being a reliable measure, an insight now known as Goodhart's law and applied far beyond economics, wherever a metric becomes a goal. He has remained an influential voice on money, regulation and the inflationary pull of ageing populations.
notes: Born 23 October 1936 in Oxford, so the birthplace is no longer left at the country. He is living, aged 89, which the closing sentence now reflects. The pithy 'when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure' is Marilyn Strathern's 1997 restatement; his own 1975 formulation is more technical.
checked: Wikipedia; LSE Financial Markets Group staff profile; LSE and Bank of England conference page for his 90th-birthday conference

name: Charles Kettering
bio: An American engineer and prolific inventor whose work reshaped the automobile and daily life. A farm boy from Ohio, he headed research at General Motors for decades and held nearly two hundred patents. His electric self-starter freed drivers from the dangerous hand crank and helped make the car practical for everyone; he also developed lighting and electrical systems, quick-drying paints and much else, and helped found a major cancer research institute. A tireless optimist about invention, he liked to say he was interested in the future because he meant to spend the rest of his life there.
checked: Britannica; Wikipedia (186 patents; GM research 1920-47); Engineering and Technology History Wiki; Quote Investigator on 'spend the rest of our lives there', which cites Kettering's own speeches of 1938 and 1939

name: Charles Montgomery
bio: A Canadian journalist and author who writes about how the design of cities shapes human happiness. Based in Vancouver, he spent years reporting on urban life and travelled the world talking to planners, psychologists and ordinary residents. The result, his book Happy City, argues with evidence from social science that the way we build streets, transport and public space powerfully affects our wellbeing, our health and our sense of connection to one another. Through writing, experiments and workshops he has become an influential advocate for designing cities around human flourishing rather than the car.
notes: Born in 1968 in North Vancouver; he grew up on a farm on Vancouver Island and lives in Vancouver.
checked: Wikipedia (Charles Montgomery, writer); charlesmontgomery.ca (his own site); BMW Guggenheim Lab contributor page

name: Charles W. Eliot
bio: An American educator who, as president of Harvard for forty years, transformed it from a small college into a modern research university and reshaped American higher education. A chemist by training, he took the helm in 1869 and introduced the elective system, letting students choose their studies, raised professional standards in law and medicine, and turned the university's ambitions outward. In retirement he edited the celebrated Harvard Classics, a five-foot shelf of great books meant to give any diligent reader a liberal education. Few individuals did more to shape how Americans go to university.
checked: Britannica; Wikipedia; Harvard's own page on Eliot's presidency; Harvard Square Library biography

name: Chuck Palahniuk
bio: An American novelist and the leading voice of a bleakly comic, transgressive strain of fiction. A former mechanic and journalist from the Pacific Northwest, he broke through with Fight Club, whose disaffected narrator and anarchic alter ego Tyler Durden became emblems of male alienation, especially after David Fincher's film. His spare, punchy, deliberately disturbing novels satirise consumer culture, loneliness and the hunger for meaning, often through shocking set pieces. Prolific and cult-adored, he has written many further books exploring the underside of modern American life.
checked: Britannica; Wikipedia; Encyclopedia.com (Contemporary Authors, b. 21 Feb 1962 Pasco, WA); Palahniuk's own account of his thirteen years at Freightliner on his Substack

name: Confucius
birthplace: Zou, state of Lu (near Qufu), China
bio: The most influential philosopher in Chinese history, whose teaching shaped the ethics and government of East Asia for two thousand years. Born into a poor family of fallen nobility in the state of Lu, he worked as a minor official and then as a teacher, gathering disciples and travelling from court to court in a vain search for a ruler who would put his ideas into practice. He preached virtue, ritual propriety, learning and respect for family, and a golden rule of not doing to others what you would not want done to yourself. His sayings, collected by followers after his death in the Analects, became the foundation of the Confucian tradition.
checked: Britannica (b. 551 BCE Qufu, state of Lu; d. 479 BCE in Lu); Wikipedia (Zou, in modern Qufu); Analects 15.23 for the negative golden rule

name: Daisetz Teitaro Suzuki
bio: A Japanese scholar and author who did more than any other single person to introduce Zen Buddhism to the West. Deeply versed in both Buddhist tradition and Western philosophy, and married to an American, he spent years in the United States and wrote prolifically in English, making the once-obscure practice of Zen accessible to Western readers. His many books shaped how the mid-twentieth-century West understood Zen, influencing artists, psychologists and the Beat writers and feeding a broad postwar fascination with Eastern spirituality. He went on lecturing and writing into his nineties.
notes: Also known as D. T. Suzuki. Britannica gives Kamakura, where he lived, as his place of death; the D. T. Suzuki Museum in Kanazawa and the Matsugaoka Bunko chronology both record that he died at St Luke's International Hospital in Tokyo on 12 July 1966.
checked: Britannica; D. T. Suzuki Museum (Kanazawa) chronology; Matsugaoka Bunko chronology; Association for Asian Studies biographical summary; Wikipedia on Beatrice Erskine Lane Suzuki

name: Dalai Lama
bio: Spiritual leader of Tibetan Buddhism and, for many, the face of Tibet itself. Recognised at the age of two as the reincarnation of his predecessor, the son of a farming family in Amdo was enthroned in Lhasa in February 1940 and assumed full temporal power only in November 1950, at fifteen, as Chinese forces advanced. After the failed Lhasa uprising of 1959 he fled across the Himalayas to India, and has led a government-in-exile and a scattered people ever since. Preaching nonviolence, compassion and dialogue between science and religion, he won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1989 and became one of the world's most recognised spiritual figures, devolving his political authority to an elected Tibetan leadership in 2011.
notes: Personal name Tenzin Gyatso.
checked: Official biography and chronology of events at dalailama.com; Central Tibetan Administration press note on the 1940 enthronement; Wikipedia

name: Dale Carnegie
bio: An American writer and lecturer who founded the modern self-improvement industry. Born poor on a Missouri farm, he tried salesmanship and acting before finding his calling teaching courses in public speaking and human relations. His 1936 book How to Win Friends and Influence People, full of practical advice on getting along with others, becoming genuinely interested in them and making them feel important, became one of the best-selling books of all time and remains in print. His courses in confidence and communication have been taken by millions, and his homely, upbeat philosophy still colours American business culture.
checked: Britannica (d. 1 Nov 1955, Forest Hills, New York); Britannica Kids; Wikipedia

name: Dale Partridge
bio: An American entrepreneur turned pastor and author, who writes on business, leadership and Reformed Christian faith. Raised in southern California, he started businesses in his late teens and in 2011 co-founded Sevenly, a retail startup that gave a share of every sale to charity; his 2015 book People Over Profit argued for honesty, generosity and purpose in commerce and reached the Wall Street Journal bestseller list. He left the business world for ministry in 2017, and since 2023 has been lead pastor of King's Way Reformed Church in Prescott, Arizona, running the digital ministry Relearn.org and Reformation Seminary and reaching a large online following.
notes: Born 10 April 1985 in Upland, California. The Library of Congress name authority gives 'Partridge, Dale, 1985-'.
checked: Library of Congress name authority (Partridge, Dale, 1985-); Wikipedia; King's Way Reformed Church staff page

name: Danielle LaPorte
bio: A Canadian author, speaker and entrepreneur in the self-help and spirituality field. Born in Windsor, Ontario, and raised in rural Essex County, she first made her name with The Fire Starter Sessions, a brisk guide to building a business and a life on one's own terms, and then with The Desire Map, which urges readers to plan their lives around how they want to feel rather than around goals and to-do lists. Through books, a popular blog, planners and 'heart-centred' training programmes she has built a large following, and her brief, punchy affirmations on desire, truth and self-worth circulate widely online.
notes: Born 25 May 1969 in Windsor, Ontario. The Library of Congress name authority (no2008097412) records the date, taken from the author herself.
checked: Library of Congress name authority no2008097412 (birth date 1969-05-25, source: email from the author); Wikipedia

name: David Foster Wallace
bio: An American novelist and essayist regarded as one of the most gifted and influential writers of his generation. The son of a philosophy professor, and himself brilliant in logic and mathematics, he wrote fiction of restless intelligence, footnoted, self-aware and morally earnest, seeking sincerity in an age of irony. His huge novel Infinite Jest, a sprawling story of addiction, entertainment and loneliness in a near-future America, became a landmark, and his essays on subjects from cruise ships to tennis are widely loved. Long tormented by depression, he took his own life at forty-six.
checked: Wikipedia; Illinois Center for the Book author record; Library of Congress name authority n86001949 (b. 21 Feb 1962, Ithaca, N.Y.); Wikipedia on James D. Wallace, philosophy professor at Illinois

name: Deepak Chopra
bio: An Indian-American physician and author, among the best-known and most-debated figures of the mind-body and New Age wellness movements. Trained as a doctor in India, he practised endocrinology in the United States before turning, in the 1980s, to alternative and 'quantum' healing, blending Ayurveda, meditation and popularised physics into a message of self-healing and consciousness. Hugely successful as a speaker and the author of dozens of best-sellers such as Ageless Body, Timeless Mind, he is embraced by a mass following and sharply criticised by scientists who see his use of physics as metaphor stretched past meaning.
notes: Birth year sometimes given as 1947: in the memoir Brotherhood he writes that he was born on 22 October 1946 and that his parents later moved his official birthday to 22 April 1947 so that he could start school on relocating.
checked: Wikipedia; Encyclopedia.com (Contemporary Authors); EBSCO research starter; Carnegie Corporation Great Immigrants profile; Deepak and Sanjiv Chopra, Brotherhood

name: Deng Ming-Dao
bio: A Chinese-American author and artist who writes accessibly about Taoism for Western readers. Born in San Francisco, he studied Taoist internal arts, meditation and martial arts for many years under a traditional master, and works also as a graphic designer and fine artist. His best-known book, 365 Tao, offers a short meditation for each day of the year, and in Everyday Tao, Scholar Warrior and the Chronicles of Tao he presents Taoist philosophy and practice through instruction and storytelling. Translated into many languages, his gentle, practical writing has introduced countless readers to the Way.
notes: 'Deng' is the family name, 'Ming-Dao' the given name.
checked: Wikipedia (b. 1954, San Francisco); publisher's author note to 365 Tao (HarperSanFrancisco, 1992); Santa Cruz Sentinel interview, 31 Jan 2013

name: Diogenes
bio: A Greek philosopher and the most notorious of the Cynics, who turned philosophy into public performance. Exiled from his native Sinope after a scandal over defacing the coinage, he came to Athens and later Corinth, where he made a virtue of extreme poverty, reputedly living in a large ceramic jar, owning almost nothing and begging his bread. He lit a lamp in broad daylight and went about saying that he was looking for a man, and mocked wealth, rank and convention as so much vanity. Invited by Alexander the Great to name any favour, he asked only that the king step out of his sunlight. His life was one long argument that virtue means living simply and shamelessly, in accord with nature.
notes: Dates approximate. Diogenes of Sinope. The lamp anecdote at Diogenes Laertius 6.41 has him say only 'I am looking for a man'; 'an honest man' is a modern embellishment found in no ancient source.
checked: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 6.20-6.41, Hicks translation via Perseus and LacusCurtius; Wikipedia

name: Dorothy Thompson
bio: An American journalist, one of the most famous of her day and a fearless early warner against fascism. Reporting from Europe between the wars, she interviewed Hitler and was, in 1934, the first American correspondent expelled from Nazi Germany. Back home she wrote a hugely popular newspaper column and broadcast to millions, campaigning against Nazism and for refugees, and was reckoned one of the most influential women in the United States. Outspoken and independent, married for a time to the novelist Sinclair Lewis, she embodied the conscience of American journalism in a dangerous age.
checked: Britannica; Wikipedia; Eleanor Roosevelt Papers Project (George Washington University); US Holocaust Memorial Museum, History Unfolded, on the August 1934 expulsion; Library of Congress name authority n85185570

name: Dwight Goddard
bio: An American Christian missionary turned Buddhist, and an early bridge between East and West. Trained as an engineer and then as a minister, he went to China as a missionary but grew disillusioned with the effort and was drawn instead to Buddhism, particularly Zen. He tried to found an American Buddhist monastic community, and is best remembered for editing A Buddhist Bible, a widely used anthology of Buddhist scriptures in English. That book, encountered by Jack Kerouac and other Beats, helped seed the mid-century American interest in Zen, giving Goddard a quiet but real influence.
checked: New York Times obituary, 9 July 1939 (b. Worcester 5 July 1861, d. Randolph Hospital, Vermont, on his 78th birthday); Worcester Polytechnic Institute finding aid to the Dwight Goddard Papers; Tricycle profile of Goddard

name: E. E. Cummings
bio: An American poet, painter and playwright known for a playful, radically inventive verse. The son of a Harvard lecturer turned Unitarian minister, he volunteered as an ambulance driver in the First World War and was then interned for three and a half months in a French detention camp on a groundless suspicion of espionage, an experience that fixed his distrust of authority and became his prose account The Enormous Room. In hundreds of poems he broke words, punctuation and typography apart and reassembled them on the page, using lower-case letters and scattered syntax to lyric, satirical and tender effect. Beneath the experiment lay an old-fashioned romantic, celebrating love, spring, the individual and the natural world.
notes: Often styled e. e. cummings.
checked: Britannica; Wikipedia; E. E. Cummings chronology compiled by Michael Webster, Grand Valley State University

name: Eckhart Tolle
bio: A German-born spiritual teacher, resident in Canada, whose books on living in the present moment have sold in the tens of millions. By his account, after years of anxiety and depression he underwent, at twenty-nine, a sudden inner transformation that dissolved his sense of a suffering self. He spent years reflecting on that shift, and later distilled it into The Power of Now and A New Earth, teaching that most human misery comes from identifying with the incessant thinking mind, and that peace is found by stepping into pure present awareness. Championed by Oprah Winfrey, he became one of the most popular spiritual authors alive.
checked: Library of Congress name authority n99054690 (birth place: Lünen (Germany); birth date 1948); Wikipedia; eckharttolle.com

name: Ed Greenwood
bio: A Canadian fantasy author, editor and game designer, best known as the creator of the Forgotten Realms. He began inventing the world as a boy in suburban Toronto, wrote it up for Dragon magazine from 1979 and sold it to TSR in 1986, after which it became the most popular setting for the Dungeons and Dragons role-playing game and the backdrop for hundreds of novels, adventures and video games. A prolific novelist and game writer who spent his working life in Ontario public libraries, and a booming, antiquarian presence at conventions, he is among the most influential figures in modern fantasy gaming and shared world-building.
notes: Born in Toronto, 21 July 1959; worked in Greater Toronto libraries from 1974 and still in library work after retiring from Toronto Public Library, so 'former librarian' was dropped.
checked: Wikipedia; Paizo interview 2010; edgreenwood.net; Tribality interview 2015

name: Edward de Bono
bio: A Maltese physician, psychologist and author who made a career out of teaching people how to think. Trained in medicine and psychology, he became famous for the idea of 'lateral thinking', the deliberate search for fresh approaches by breaking away from habitual, logical steps, a phrase he coined that entered the dictionary. Through dozens of books, among them Six Thinking Hats, and courses taken up by schools and corporations, he promoted structured tools for creativity and decision-making. Enormously popular and much imitated, he was dismissed by some academics but did more than most to popularise creative thinking.
notes: Guardian obituary gives St Julian's Bay, Malta as birthplace and his home in Malta as where he died; the Library of Congress authority record has only 'Malta'. Death date disputed: Guardian, Telegraph and the de Bono Group give 9 June 2021, Wikipedia 10 June 2021.
checked: Guardian obituary 10 June 2021; Telegraph obituary 10 June 2021; Library of Congress name authority n79060619; University of Malta notice 2021; debonogroup.com

name: Edward Ericson
bio: An American literary scholar, for twenty-six years a professor of English at Calvin College in Grand Rapids, Michigan, and one of the leading Western interpreters of Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn. Trained on Milton and seventeenth-century English literature, he turned to the Russian dissident after reading his novels for pleasure, argued in Solzhenitsyn: The Moral Vision and Solzhenitsyn and the Modern World that the work is inseparable from its author's Orthodox Christian faith, and prepared the authorised one-volume abridgement of The Gulag Archipelago, revising it in 1983 side by side with Solzhenitsyn himself. He later co-edited The Solzhenitsyn Reader.
notes: Identity settled: Edward E. Ericson Jr., born Chicago 19 October 1939, died Siloam Springs, Arkansas, 29 April 2017; taught at Hope, Westmont and Northwestern before Calvin College, 1977-2003. His life is well recorded, so the earlier bio's caution about that was removed; the quotation credited to him in the bank is still unsourced.
checked: Herald-Leader (Siloam Springs) obituary 3 May 2017; Calvin University memorial notice 2 May 2017; Acton Institute Religion & Liberty; ISI edition notes to The Solzhenitsyn Reader; Harper abridged Gulag Archipelago 1985

name: Edward Gibbon
bio: An English historian whose The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire is one of the masterpieces of the language. A sickly, bookish boy, the only one of seven children to survive infancy, and left with independent means, he conceived the work, he said, while musing amid the ruins of Rome. Over more than a decade he traced the fall of Rome and the thousand-year sequel of Byzantium in six magisterial volumes, marked by vast learning, a stately, ironic prose and a famously sceptical eye toward the early church. Controversial in its own day and still read for its style, the book set a lasting standard for narrative history.
notes: Not an only child: he was the eldest of seven, the rest dying in infancy. Died at his lodgings in St James's Street, London, on 16 January 1794 and was buried at Fletching, Sussex, so the London deathplace stands.
checked: Britannica; EBSCO research starter; Lord Sheffield's note appended to Gibbon's Memoirs; Wikipedia

name: Edwin Chapin
bio: An American Universalist minister, preacher and writer, born Edwin Hubbell Chapin. From 1848 he led a Universalist congregation in New York City, later named the Church of the Divine Paternity, and was one of the best-known public speakers of his time. His sermons and lectures on social reform, temperance and moral duty were published in many volumes, and short sayings taken from them circulate as quotations.
checked: Written from general reference knowledge on 2026-09-29 without access to sources; to be verified.

name: Elbert Hubbard
deathplace: At sea off the Old Head of Kinsale, Ireland (aboard the Lusitania)
bio: An American writer, publisher and craftsman, a leading figure of the American Arts and Crafts movement. A successful soap salesman who reinvented himself, he founded the Roycroft community of artisans in East Aurora, New York, printing finely made books and magazines. He is best remembered for A Message to Garcia, a short, hugely popular essay praising the employee who quietly gets a hard job done without excuses. A tireless self-promoter and epigrammatist, he died with his wife aboard the Lusitania when a German submarine sank it in 1915.
notes: The Lusitania was torpedoed about 11 miles off the Old Head of Kinsale in the Celtic Sea, not in the Atlantic; both Hubbards were lost there on 7 May 1915.
