name: Eleanor Roosevelt
bio: An American writer, diplomat and activist, the longest-serving First Lady of the United States and one of the most admired women of the twentieth century. A shy orphan who married her cousin Franklin, she transformed the role of presidential wife, holding press conferences, writing a daily newspaper column and travelling as his eyes and ears through his long presidency. A tireless champion of the poor, of workers, women and civil rights, she went on after his death to chair the United Nations commission that drafted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
checked: Britannica; FDR Presidential Library and Museum biography; Wikipedia

name: Elie Wiesel
bio: A Romanian-born American writer and human-rights activist who became the world's foremost witness to the Holocaust. Deported as a teenager to Auschwitz and Buchenwald, where his father, mother and a sister died, he survived and, after years of silence, distilled the horror into the slender, shattering memoir Night. He went on to write dozens more books and spent his life speaking out against genocide, hatred and indifference, insisting that the world must remember. He won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1986 and helped bring into being the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum.
checked: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia; NobelPrize.org biographical; Britannica; Buchenwald Memorial biography

name: Elisabeth Kübler-Ross
bio: A Swiss-American psychiatrist who changed the way the modern world thinks about death. Working with dying patients in American hospitals at a time when their needs were often ignored, she listened to them and wrote the landmark book On Death and Dying, which set out five stages of grief, denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance. A pioneer of the hospice and palliative-care movement, she argued that the terminally ill have much to teach the living, and spent her career urging doctors and families to face death with honesty and compassion.
checked: Britannica; US National Library of Medicine, Changing the Face of Medicine; Elisabeth Kübler-Ross Foundation; Wikipedia

name: Emil Boc
bio: A Romanian politician and academic who has served as prime minister of Romania and, for many years, as mayor of the city of Cluj-Napoca. Trained in law and political science, he became a university lecturer before entering politics on the centre-right. As prime minister during the financial crisis he oversaw harsh austerity measures, but as long-serving mayor of Cluj he won wide praise for turning the city into one of Romania's most dynamic, a hub of technology, culture and student life. He is seen as one of the country's most durable and consequential local leaders.
checked: Wikipedia; Boc's CV at the Babeș-Bolyai University faculty of political science; European Commission speaker page

name: Enrique Peñalosa
bio: A Colombian politician and urban thinker, twice mayor of Bogota, known around the world for rebuilding a city around its people rather than its cars. During his terms he created a pioneering bus rapid-transit network, hundreds of kilometres of protected bicycle lanes, parks, libraries and wide pedestrian promenades, arguing that a good city is one where a child on a bicycle is safe and that public space is where democratic equality is lived out. A tireless advocate and lecturer, he has become an influential global voice for fair, sustainable and human-scaled urban design.
notes: Colombian politician, born in Washington, D.C., where his father was posted.
checked: Wikipedia; Habitat III speaker page; Penn IUR profile; Project for Public Spaces 2004 (tricycle-or-bicycle line); Noticias Caracol profile 2015

name: Epictetus
bio: A Greek Stoic philosopher who taught that freedom lies not in our circumstances but in the mind. Born a slave in Phrygia and left lame, he studied Stoicism while still enslaved, was freed after the death of Nero, and later founded an influential school at Nicopolis. He wrote nothing himself; his pupil Arrian preserved the Discourses and the pocket handbook, the Enchiridion. Their heart is a sharp line between what is 'up to us', our judgements and choices, and what is not, over which we should waste no grief. His thought guided Marcus Aurelius and, much later, helped inspire modern cognitive therapy.
checked: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy; Dickinson College Commentaries on the Encheiridion

name: Epicurus
bio: A Greek philosopher who founded one of the most influential schools of antiquity. Born on the island of Samos, he settled in Athens and taught in a private house and garden, welcoming women and slaves among his followers, who called themselves the friends of the Garden. He held that the aim of life is pleasure, but understood as tranquillity: the absence of bodily pain and mental disturbance, reached through simple living, friendship and the study of nature. He taught that the world is made only of atoms and void, that the gods do not meddle in human affairs, and that death is nothing to fear.
checked: Britannica; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; Diogenes Laertius, Lives 10 (LacusCurtius)

name: Erasmus von Rotterdam
bio: A Dutch humanist, priest and scholar, the leading intellectual of the northern Renaissance. The illegitimate son of a priest, he became the most celebrated man of letters in Europe, writing in an elegant Latin and travelling from city to city. He produced the first published Greek edition of the New Testament, urging a return to the sources of Christianity, and in the witty satire In Praise of Folly he mocked the corruption and superstition of the church. Though his criticism helped prepare the Reformation, he broke with Luther and pleaded throughout for tolerance and moderation.
notes: Desiderius Erasmus of Rotterdam.
checked: Britannica; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; Encyclopedia.com (New Catholic Encyclopedia); Wikipedia

name: Eric Hoffer
bio: An American social philosopher known as 'the longshoreman philosopher'. Largely self-taught, he lost his sight as a child and regained it as a teenager, then lived for decades as an itinerant labourer and, later, a dockworker in San Francisco, reading voraciously and thinking in his spare hours. His first and most famous book, The True Believer, is a penetrating study of mass movements and the psychology of fanaticism, admired across the political spectrum. He wrote a series of aphoristic books, and late in life received the Presidential Medal of Freedom.
notes: Birth year uncertain; he gave 1902, but 1898 is often cited.
checked: Britannica; New York Times obituary 22 May 1983; Hoover Institution, The Longshoreman Philosopher

name: Erich Fromm
bio: A German-American social psychologist, psychoanalyst and humanist philosopher. Trained in sociology and psychoanalysis and shaped by both Freud and Marx, he fled Nazi Germany for the United States, where he became a widely read public intellectual. He explored how societies mould character, and in Escape from Freedom argued that the burden of modern freedom can drive people into the arms of authoritarianism. His best-known book, The Art of Loving, treats love not as a lucky feeling but as a skill and a discipline to be learned. He preached a sane, life-affirming humanism.
checked: Wikipedia; Encyclopedia.com; Rainer Funk, Life and Work of Erich Fromm (Logos)

name: Erich Kästner
bio: A German writer, poet and satirist, and one of the most beloved of the twentieth century. Trained as a teacher in his native Dresden, he made his name in Weimar-era Berlin with sharp, funny, socially critical light verse and with the children's classic Emil and the Detectives, still among the most popular books ever written in German. An outspoken pacifist, he watched the Nazis burn his books in 1933 yet chose to remain in Germany, writing on under bans and pseudonyms. After the war he returned to children's stories, poetry and journalism, defending reason, decency and a gentle, clear-eyed humanism.
checked: German and English Wikipedia; Erich Kästner Museum Dresden chronology (kaestnerhaus-literatur.de); Stadt Dresden Kästner timeline

name: Forrest Church
bio: An American theologian and minister, for many years the leader of a prominent Unitarian Universalist congregation in New York. The son of a United States senator, he combined a scholar's training in the history of religion with a pastor's gift for plain speech, and wrote some two dozen books on faith, freedom and mortality. He is remembered for a simple, much-quoted definition of religion as our human response to the dual reality of being alive and having to die, and for the grace with which he faced his own terminal cancer, writing on how the knowledge of death can deepen life.
notes: Born in Palo Alto while his father was a student at Stanford Law School; the family moved to Boise in 1950, and the New York Times and Washington Post obituaries give Boise as the birthplace.
checked: Wikipedia; Stanford Magazine profile; New York Times obituary 26 September 2009; Washington Post obituary 28 September 2009; UUA and UUMA memorial notices

name: Francis Bacon
bio: An English philosopher, statesman and essayist, a principal architect of the scientific method. Rising to become Lord Chancellor under James I before falling from office over bribery charges, he pursued in parallel a revolution in knowledge. Against reliance on ancient authority and pure logic, he argued that truth about nature must be built up patiently from observation and experiment, a programme set out in his Novum Organum. His pithy, worldly Essays remain widely read. Often called the father of empiricism, he helped lay the groundwork for modern experimental science.
notes: The philosopher and statesman, not the twentieth-century painter. He died at Arundel House in Highgate, then in Middlesex, outside the city of London.
checked: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; Wikipedia; EBSCO research starter; Online Library of Liberty

name: Francis of Assisi
bio: An Italian friar and mystic, one of the most beloved saints in Christian history and the founder of the Franciscan order. The son of a rich cloth merchant, he abandoned his wealth after a series of spiritual awakenings to embrace radical poverty, begging, preaching and tending lepers and the poor. He gathered followers into a new kind of religious order, sworn to own nothing, and is said to have received the stigmata, the wounds of Christ. Famous for his tenderness toward animals and all creation, celebrated in his Canticle of the Sun, he is the patron saint of ecology.
checked: Britannica; Catholic Encyclopedia (New Advent); New Catholic Encyclopedia via Encyclopedia.com; Wikipedia

name: Francis Paul Wilson
bio: An American author of horror, science fiction and thrillers, and a physician by training. A prolific storyteller, he is best known for the Repairman Jack novels, featuring an urban mercenary who fixes problems outside the law, and for the classic horror novel The Keep, set in a haunted castle during the Second World War. He has written across many genres and built a large interconnected 'Secret History' linking much of his fiction. Popular with genre readers and a fixture of the field for decades, he practised medicine for years alongside his writing.
checked: Wikipedia; Contemporary Authors entry at Encyclopedia.com; the author's own site, repairmanjack.com

name: Frank Zappa
bio: An American composer, guitarist and bandleader of ferocious originality and output. Self-taught and omnivorous, he led the Mothers of Invention and a long line of virtuoso bands through rock, jazz, doo-wop and orchestral music, all laced with absurdist satire of American life and hypocrisy. Fiercely independent, he controlled his own recordings and released dozens of albums; a rare abstainer from drugs, he testified memorably before the United States Senate against the labelling and censorship of music. Prolific to the end, he died of cancer at fifty-two, admired as both a clown and a serious composer.
checked: Britannica; Wikipedia; transcript of his statement to the Senate Commerce Committee, 19 September 1985 (American Rhetoric)

name: Franz Kafka
bio: A German-language writer from Prague whose name has become an adjective for the nightmarish and absurd. A Jewish insurance official who wrote at night, he published little in his lifetime and asked that his manuscripts be burned; his friend Max Brod disobeyed, saving the novels The Trial and The Castle and stories such as The Metamorphosis. In them ordinary people are trapped in vast, opaque systems of law, bureaucracy and guilt whose logic they can never grasp, all rendered in cool, precise, dreamlike prose. Dead of tuberculosis at forty, he is now seen as one of the central writers of his century.
notes: Prague was in Austria-Hungary at his birth.
checked: Wikipedia; Franz Kafka Museum Prague timeline; YIVO Encyclopedia

name: Fred Kent
bio: An American urbanist and placemaking advocate, the founder of the nonprofit Project for Public Spaces. A student of the sociologist William H. Whyte, whose patient filming of how people use city plazas shaped his outlook, he devoted his career to helping communities create lively, welcoming public squares, parks and streets. He championed the idea that great places are made not by grand design but by attending to how ordinary people actually gather, sit and linger, and that the place should come before the project. His ideas have shaped how cities around the world treat their shared spaces.
notes: Project for Public Spaces marked his seventy-fifth birthday on 2 November 2017, which puts his birth in 1942; a profile of March 2002 gives his age as 58, which would make it 1943. Birthplace not on record; he grew up in Andover, Massachusetts, and moved to West Hartford, Connecticut, as a teenager.
checked: Project for Public Spaces, 'Celebrating 75 Years of Fred Kent' (2 November 2017) and his PPS staff page; Landscape Architecture Magazine profile, March 2002; PlacemakingX profile; Wikipedia

name: Friedrich Nietzsche
bio: A German philosopher whose radical, aphoristic writing has shaken Western thought ever since. A brilliant young classical scholar made a professor at twenty-four, he left academia for a wandering life of ill health and ferocious productivity. He proclaimed that 'God is dead', meaning that the old religious foundations of morality had crumbled, and challenged humanity to create its own values rather than sink into nihilism. His ideas, the will to power, the eternal recurrence, the overman and the critique of herd morality, pour out of books such as Thus Spoke Zarathustra. He collapsed into madness at forty-four.
notes: Röcken, now part of Lützen, was in the Prussian Province of Saxony at his birth.
checked: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Nietzsche's Life and Works'; Wikipedia

name: Future Islands
bio: An American synth-pop band, not a person, formed in 2006 in North Carolina and later based in Baltimore. Built around driving synthesizers and bass, the group is defined above all by its singer Samuel T. Herring, whose raw, theatrical baritone and intensely physical performances set it apart. After years of touring the underground, they broke through in 2014 with the song 'Seasons (Waiting on You)' and a spellbinding television debut that went viral. Their music pairs propulsive, danceable arrangements with lyrics of longing, memory and emotional honesty, winning a devoted following.
notes: A band, credited for a song lyric; fronted by Samuel T. Herring.
checked: Wikipedia; AllMusic; Baltimore Banner interview with the band; Daily Beast profile, March 2014

name: G. Kingsley Ward
bio: A Canadian chartered accountant turned entrepreneur, remembered for a bestselling book of fatherly counsel. Raised in Bathurst, New Brunswick, he qualified at Price Waterhouse, bought two pharmaceutical companies and went on to chair a string of private and public firms through the Vimy Ridge Group he founded in 1982. Letters he had written to his son about work, integrity and ambition were published in 1985 as Letters of a Businessman to His Son, became an international bestseller and were followed by further volumes, among them Letters of a Businessman to His Daughter. He also co-edited Courage Remembered, an account of the Commonwealth war cemeteries, and served as honorary colonel of a New Brunswick regiment.
notes: Born 29 August 1932, died 17 August 2014; the obituary does not name where he died, and the funeral was held in Aurora, Ontario.
checked: Obituary in the National Post and Globe and Mail, August 2014; VRG Capital company page; Manitoba Library Association review of the 1985 Collins edition of Letters of a Businessman to His Son; Doull Books catalogue

name: Gaston Bachelard
bio: A French philosopher who wrote, unusually, on both science and poetry. Largely self-taught and a late starter, he became a leading philosopher of science, arguing that knowledge advances not smoothly but by 'epistemological breaks' that overturn earlier intuitions. In a second career he turned to the imagination, exploring in books such as The Psychoanalysis of Fire and The Poetics of Space how the mind dreams through the four elements and through houses, corners and shells. His subtle, lyrical writing on reverie and daydream shaped later literary theory and how we think about creativity and place.
checked: Wikipedia; Encyclopedia.com (Dictionary of Scientific Biography and Encyclopedia of Philosophy entries); EBSCO research starter

name: George Bernard Shaw
bio: An Irish playwright, critic and polemicist, the most important English-language dramatist since Shakespeare and a tireless public provocateur. Largely self-educated, he moved to London, championed Ibsen and Wagner as a critic, and in 1884 joined the newly formed socialist Fabian Society, wrote its first manifesto and became its leading pamphleteer. In more than sixty witty, argumentative plays, among them Pygmalion, Man and Superman and Saint Joan, he used comedy to attack hypocrisy, poverty, war and conventional morality. A lifelong campaigner and vegetarian famous for his paradoxes, he won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1925.
checked: Wikipedia; Edward R. Pease, The History of the Fabian Society (Project Gutenberg); Fabian Tract No. 2 (1884) at the Online Library of Liberty

name: George E. Miller
bio: An American physician who left clinical medicine for the study of how doctors are taught. After running a project in medical education at the University at Buffalo, he founded the Office of Research in Medical Education at the University of Illinois College of Medicine in 1959, among the first of its kind and a model copied by medical schools around the world, and went on to direct its successor, the Center for Educational Development. A paper of 1990 on the assessment of clinical skills set out the four ascending levels, 'knows', 'knows how', 'shows how' and 'does', still taught everywhere as Miller's pyramid, though his name is far less widely known than the diagram.
notes: Born 19 June 1919, died 7 November 1998. Birthplace not given in the published memorial notices. More than one public figure bears this name, so a quotation credited simply to 'George E. Miller' needs care.
checked: Wikipedia; Miller, 'The assessment of clinical skills/competence/performance', Academic Medicine 65 (1990); Cruess et al., 'Amending Miller's Pyramid', Academic Medicine 2016; 'Nonphysician Medical Educators', Academic Medicine 2009; citation records for the 1999 memorial notices by Christine McGuire

name: George Lois
bio: An American advertising art director and designer, a leading figure of the 'creative revolution' that transformed Madison Avenue in the 1960s. The son of Greek immigrants, he was famous for bold, witty, idea-driven campaigns, and above all for a run of provocative covers he designed for Esquire magazine, images that captured the turmoil of the era and are now studied as landmarks of graphic design. Combative and self-promoting, he claimed credit for slogans and campaigns that entered the culture, and preached that great advertising is an art form.
checked: New York Times obituary 19 November 2022; Washington Post obituary 21 November 2022; Associated Press obituary; City College of New York memorial notice; Wikipedia

name: George Sheehan
bio: An American cardiologist and writer who became the philosopher of the running boom. A busy doctor and father of twelve, he took up running again in middle age and found in it a path to self-discovery, then wrote about it in newspaper columns and best-selling books such as Running and Being. Blending sports advice with reflections drawn from the classics and his own experience, he treated the daily run as a spiritual and philosophical practice, a way to become the person one was meant to be. He kept writing about mortality and meaning as he faced his own final illness.
checked: New York Times obituary, 2 November 1993; georgesheehan.com biography; English Wikipedia

name: Gloria Steinem
bio: An American journalist and activist, one of the most recognisable leaders of the twentieth-century women's movement. After an unsettled childhood in Ohio, she became a magazine writer, drawing attention with an undercover expose of a Playboy Club, then emerged as a spokeswoman for feminism, co-founding Ms. magazine and a string of women's organisations. A gifted speaker and organiser, she campaigned for reproductive rights, equal pay and an end to discrimination, and remained an activist into her later decades, doing much to carry feminist ideas into the American mainstream.
checked: Britannica; National Women's History Museum biography; gloriasteinem.com; NYU Undercover Reporting archive of 'A Bunny's Tale' (Show, 1963)

name: Gottfried von Jacquin
bio: An Austrian civil servant with a fine bass voice, an amateur composer, and one of the closest friends of Mozart's Vienna years. The son of the botanist Nikolaus Joseph von Jacquin, whose house in the botanical garden was a gathering place for the city's scientific and musical society, he held a post at the Bohemian court chancellery and received some of the warmest and funniest letters Mozart ever wrote, sent from Prague in 1787. Mozart composed the bass aria 'Mentre ti lascio, o figlia' for him, and let him publish two songs of Mozart's own, among them 'Das Traumbild', under his name, so that several pieces long passed as his work. He died in Vienna in January 1792, seven weeks after Mozart, and is recalled for the light he throws on Mozart's private world rather than for anything of his own.
notes: Born at Schemnitz in Hungary, where his father held the chair of mining sciences until 1768, not at Vienna. No day or month of birth is recorded, so his age at death is given variously as 24 and 25, and the bio names neither.
checked: Kalliope union catalogue / GND authority record 130187801 (Banska Stiavnica - 24.01.1792 Vienna); Oesterreichisches Musiklexikon, Jacquin family; Cambridge Mozart Encyclopedia (Eisen and Keefe); Mozarteum digital edition of Mozart's letters to Jacquin, 1787; Grove, A Dictionary of Music and Musicians

name: Harriet Woods
bio: An American politician and advocate from Missouri, a trailblazer for women in public life. She came to politics through local activism in University City, where a complaint about a rattling manhole cover led to a seat on the city council, and went on to the state senate in 1976 and then, in 1984, to election as lieutenant governor, the first woman to win statewide office in Missouri. She ran twice for the United States Senate and lost both races narrowly, to John Danforth in 1982 by some 27,000 votes of 1.5 million, and to Christopher Bond in 1986; the first defeat, when she ran out of money for television advertising in the closing weeks, prompted the founding of EMILY's List. She later served as president of the National Women's Political Caucus, working to bring more women into elected office.
notes: Her name is spelled Harriett in her own records and in the obituaries. She died at her home in University City, a municipality in St Louis County, not in St Louis itself. Only the 1982 Senate defeat preceded her election as lieutenant governor; the second came in 1986, two years after it. The saying about standing tall without standing on someone cannot be traced to her beyond quote anthologies, so the bio no longer credits it to her.
checked: New York Times obituary, 10 February 2007; Washington Post obituary, 10 February 2007; Los Angeles Times, 12 February 2007; State Historical Society of Missouri, Historic Missourians; Missouri State Archives finding aid RG4.42; English Wikipedia

name: Heath Ledger
bio: An Australian actor of rare intensity who achieved great fame before his early death. Growing up in Perth, he moved to the United States and broke through as a heartthrob before deliberately turning to darker, more demanding roles. His tender, tormented cowboy in Brokeback Mountain won wide acclaim, and his terrifying, anarchic Joker in The Dark Knight became one of the most celebrated screen villains ever. He died of an accidental prescription-drug overdose at twenty-eight, while The Dark Knight was in post-production, and was awarded a posthumous Academy Award for the role.
checked: New York Times, 22 January 2008 and 23 February 2009; ABC News, 23 February 2009; English Wikipedia

name: Hecato of Rhodes
bio: A Greek Stoic philosopher of the island of Rhodes and a pupil of Panaetius, the head of the Stoic school. He wrote extensively on ethics, on duties, virtues, goods and the paradoxes of moral progress, and was clearly a figure of standing in his day. None of his writing survives; he is known only through references and quotations in later authors, above all Cicero's On Duties and Seneca's essays, where several of his pointed sayings on friendship, gratitude and self-sufficiency are preserved, including lines that Seneca reworks in his Letters.
notes: Flourished around 100 BC; dates approximate.
checked: Cicero, De Officiis 3.15 and 3.63 (Perseus); Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7 (the list of treatises); Seneca, Epistulae morales 9 and De Beneficiis; Smith, Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography; 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica (Wikisource)

name: Heinz Stucke
bio: A German long-distance cyclist who spent more than half a century pedalling around the world. In 1962, at twenty-two, he quit his job as a toolmaker in his hometown of Hovelhof and rode away on a three-speed bicycle, and simply kept going, covering some 600,000 kilometres across more than a hundred countries over five decades, financing the journey by selling booklets and photographs of his travels. Robbed, jailed and injured many times, he became a legend among world travellers before finally settling back in the town he had left, where he died at eighty-six.
notes: Died 22 July 2026.
checked: English Wikipedia; Gemeinde Hoevelhof obituary notice; Adventure Cycling Association obituary, 3 August 2026; Bicycle Network, 28 July 2026; Bikepacking.com tribute, July 2026

name: Helen Keller
bio: An American author, lecturer and activist who became a worldwide symbol of the triumph of will over disability. Left deaf and blind by an illness before she was two, she lived cut off from language until the teacher Anne Sullivan broke through to her at the water pump, spelling words into her hand, a scene made famous by The Miracle Worker. Keller went on to graduate from Radcliffe College, the first deaf-blind person to earn a degree, and to write books and campaign around the globe for the blind, for women's suffrage, for workers and for peace.
notes: Arcan Ridge, the house she died in, stands in Easton; the American Foundation for the Blind and Britannica give the place of death as Westport, its postal address, which is where the discrepancy comes from.
checked: Perkins School for the Blind timeline; American Foundation for the Blind biography and chronology; Britannica; University of Alabama, Alabama Authors record; English Wikipedia

name: Helen Schucman
bio: An American research psychologist and the scribe of A Course in Miracles. A professor of medical psychology at Columbia University and, by her own account, a sceptical non-believer, she began in 1965 to experience an inner voice dictating text, which she wrote down over several years with the help of a colleague. The result, published as A Course in Miracles, became an influential work of modern spirituality, teaching forgiveness and the healing of the mind through love. Uneasy about her strange role, she kept her authorship quiet in her lifetime, and it became widely known only later.
checked: Library of Congress name authority record n91013548; Wikidata Q273262; Encyclopedia.com; English Wikipedia

name: Henri Poincaré
bio: A French mathematician, physicist and philosopher, the last man said to have commanded the whole of mathematics in his time. He made foundational contributions across the field, founded the discipline of topology, and in studying the three-body problem of celestial mechanics glimpsed the sensitive dependence on starting conditions later called chaos. He came remarkably close to special relativity before Einstein, and wrote widely read books on science and method reflecting on the role of intuition and convention in discovery. His cousin Raymond served as president of France during the First World War.
checked: Britannica; MacTutor History of Mathematics biography (St Andrews); English Wikipedia

name: Henri-Dominique Lacordaire
bio: A French Dominican friar and preacher who revived his order in France after the Revolution. Trained as a lawyer and once a religious sceptic, he underwent a dramatic conversion, took holy orders, and became the most celebrated preacher of his age, filling the cathedral of Notre-Dame in Paris. A champion of liberal Catholicism who tried to reconcile the church with modern freedoms, he re-established the Dominican order on French soil. He is often quoted for the paradox that between the strong and the weak it is liberty that oppresses and the law that sets free.
notes: The saying about the strong and the weak is genuine and primary: 'entre le fort et le faible, entre le riche et le pauvre, entre le maitre et le serviteur, c'est la liberte qui opprime, et la loi qui affranchit', from the 52nd Conference de Notre-Dame, 'Du double travail de l'homme', preached 16 April 1848 and printed in Oeuvres, tome IV, pp. 490-494; the ledger's note calling it absent from the Conferences is mistaken.
checked: Britannica; Catholic Encyclopedia; Encyclopedia.com; Oeuvres du R. P. Henri-Dominique Lacordaire, Conferences de Notre-Dame de Paris, tome IV (Gallica, BnF); Louis Garriguet, Le contrat de travail (1904), p. 76, via Internet Archive full-text search; English Wikipedia

name: Henry 'Red' Sanders
bio: An American college football coach, best remembered for a single famous saying. Born in Asheville, North Carolina, and raised in Nashville, he played quarterback at Vanderbilt, came back to coach there in two spells either side of wartime service in the Navy, and then took over at UCLA, where his single-wing team went unbeaten in 1954 and was named national champion by the coaches' poll. He was known for a hard-driving manner, a sharp tongue and an unusually light practice week. He is credited as the true source of the line that winning isn't everything, it's the only thing, first recorded from him in 1948 and later made famous by, and often attributed to, the professional coach Vince Lombardi. He died of a heart attack at fifty-three, his name preserved chiefly by that much-repeated maxim.
notes: Born at Asheville, North Carolina; he was raised in Nashville from boyhood and buried there, which is where the birthplace error comes from. He was fifty-three at his death, not fifty-two.
checked: College Football Hall of Fame inductee record (born Asheville, 7 May 1905); English Wikipedia; Los Angeles Times, 13 August 2018; UPI notice of 19 August 1958; Quote Investigator, 'Winning Isn't Everything; It's the Only Thing' (earliest instance the Birmingham News, 9 November 1948)

name: Henry Cloud
bio: An American clinical psychologist, leadership consultant and author, best known for the hugely popular book Boundaries, written with John Townsend. He grew up in Vicksburg, Mississippi, and was recruited to Southern Methodist University to play golf; a hand injury ended that ambition and turned him toward faith and psychology, and he took a doctorate in clinical psychology at Biola University in 1987. Drawing on psychology and Christian teaching, Boundaries and its many follow-ups argue that healthy relationships depend on knowing where one person ends and another begins, and on the courage to say no. He has since written widely on leadership, character and personal growth, hosted a radio show for fifteen years, and works as an executive coach; his books have sold many millions of copies.
notes: Born at Vicksburg, Mississippi, on the evidence of the Christian Broadcasting Network's guest biography and the German Wikipedia article; English Wikipedia records the year alone. His childhood illness, his golf career at Southern Methodist and his doctorate at Biola are all on record, so the bio no longer says little of his life is known.
checked: Christian Broadcasting Network guest biography ('born and raised in Vicksburg, Mississippi'); boundariesbooks.com and drcloud.com official biographies; German Wikipedia; English Wikipedia; Internet Archive full-text search

name: Henry David Thoreau
bio: An American essayist, poet and naturalist, a leading light of Transcendentalism and a founder of modern nature writing. He spent most of his short life in his native Concord, Massachusetts, working odd jobs and observing the natural world with great care. For two years he lived alone in a cabin he built beside Walden Pond, an experiment in simple, deliberate living that became his masterpiece, Walden. Jailed briefly for refusing a tax that funded slavery and the Mexican War, he defended the individual conscience against the state in the essay Civil Disobedience, which later inspired Gandhi and Martin Luther King.
checked: Britannica; The Thoreau Society, Thoreau's Life; Walden Woods Project chronology; English Wikipedia

name: Henry Miller
bio: An American writer whose frank, exuberant, autobiographical novels helped break the modern taboo on sexual candour. Born in New York and long adrift in odd jobs, he moved to Paris in his late thirties and there found his voice in Tropic of Cancer, a raw, freewheeling account of a hungry writer's bohemian life. Banned as obscene for decades in Britain and the United States, his books finally cleared the courts in the 1960s, a landmark for literary freedom. Beyond the notoriety he was a joyous, philosophical writer, celebrating art, appetite and the liberated self.
checked: Britannica; Encyclopedia.com; English Wikipedia

name: Heraclitus
bio: A Greek philosopher of Ephesus, one of the most original of the thinkers who came before Socrates. Aristocratic, solitary and scornful of his fellow citizens, he wrote a single book, now lost, whose deliberately riddling fragments earned him the nickname 'the Obscure'. He taught that everything is in ceaseless flux, that one cannot step into the same river twice, and that the world is an ever-living fire, ordered by a hidden logos or reason. Reality, for him, is a tension of opposites, strife and harmony being one; the way up and the way down, he wrote, are one and the same.
checked: Britannica (Heraclitus); Routledge Encyclopedia of Philosophy A055; Encyclopaedia of the Hellenic World, Asia Minor (lemma 8380); Wikipedia

name: Herbert Swope
deathplace: New York City, New York, USA
bio: An American journalist and editor, the first winner of the Pulitzer Prize for reporting. A star reporter for the New York World, he covered the First World War from Germany, and the dispatches gathered as 'Inside the German Empire' took that first prize in 1917; as the paper's executive editor from 1920 he directed its campaigns against the Ku Klux Klan and New York's crime rackets and built the first modern op-ed page. The phrase 'cold war' was his, written into the speech Bernard Baruch delivered in April 1947, though it was Baruch and Walter Lippmann who carried it into common use. He is often quoted for his rueful formula for failure: that while he could not give a sure recipe for success, the surest recipe for failure is trying to please everybody.
notes: Died at Doctors Hospital in Manhattan of pneumonia after abdominal surgery (UPI dispatch, 20 June 1958); the private funeral was held from his Sands Point home, which is why Britannica and other reference works give Sands Point as the place of death. On 'cold war': Baruch's own autobiography and Respectfully Quoted credit the coinage to Swope, but the words are older - Orwell used them in October 1945 - so the earlier bio had it backwards in calling him the populariser who perhaps coined it.
checked: Britannica; Wikipedia; Encyclopaedia Judaica via Encyclopedia.com; UPI obituary in the Atlanta Daily World, 21 June 1958; Respectfully Quoted (1989) no. 233; American Heritage, 'Naming the New War' (1997); AlliiertenMuseum, 'Cold War - the (pre)history of a term'

name: Hermann Hesse
bio: A German-Swiss novelist and poet whose books trace the pull between spirit and the senses and the lonely search for one's true self. Raised in a strict Swabian missionary family against which he rebelled, he drew on that conflict throughout his work. Novels such as Demian, Siddhartha, set in the India of the Buddha, Steppenwolf and The Glass Bead Game follow seekers torn between discipline and desire, East and West. A pacifist who moved to Switzerland and opposed both world wars, he won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1946 and was rediscovered, decades on, as a hero of the 1960s counterculture.
checked: Britannica; Nobel Foundation biographical note (Literature 1946); Wikipedia

name: Honoré de Balzac
bio: A French novelist and playwright, one of the founders of literary realism. Born at Tours and pushed toward the law, he chose letters instead, and after early failures and ruinous ventures in printing wrote at a furious pace, sustained by black coffee and mounting debt. His great work is La Comedie humaine, an interlinked cycle of ninety-odd novels and stories peopled by some two thousand characters, several hundred of whom return from book to book, which set out to record every class and corner of post-Napoleonic France. Minutely observed and driven by money and ambition, books such as Old Goriot and Lost Illusions became a model for the novelists who followed.
notes: The cycle holds 91 finished works and roughly two thousand invented characters, of which counts put 460 to 573 in more than one book; the earlier bio described all two thousand as recurring.
checked: Britannica; Wikipedia (Honore de Balzac; La Comedie humaine); Encyclopaedia Universalis, 'L'univers de La Comedie humaine'; Cerfberr and Christophe, Repertory of the Comedie Humaine, prefatory note (Wikisource)

name: Hunter S. Thompson
bio: An American journalist and author, the inventor of 'Gonzo' journalism, in which the reporter drops all pretence of detachment and becomes the story's wild center. After a first book that saw him beaten by the Hells Angels he had ridden with for a year, he found his voice in the drug-soaked, hallucinatory Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas and in savage political reporting for Rolling Stone. Profane, paranoid and often brilliant, his writing fused fact, invention and fury at American hypocrisy. He lived for decades on a fortified ranch in Colorado, guns close at hand, and took his own life in 2005.
checked: Britannica; Wikipedia (Hunter S. Thompson; Hell's Angels); Random House publication record for Hell's Angels

name: Hélder Câmara
bio: A Brazilian Catholic archbishop who became one of the great voices for the poor of Latin America. As archbishop of Olinda and Recife in the impoverished northeast, he denounced hunger, inequality and the abuses of Brazil's military dictatorship, preaching nonviolence and the social mission of the church, and helped inspire what became liberation theology. Small, ascetic and fearless, he was silenced at home and honoured abroad, and was several times proposed for the Nobel Peace Prize. He is famous for asking why, when he gave the poor food he was called a saint, but when he asked why they were poor he was called a communist.
notes: He died at the three-room house behind the church in Recife where he lived after refusing the episcopal residence (Independent obituary, 1999; Irish Times, 11 September 1999); Britannica and the Reuters death notice give Olinda, which is where he was buried.
checked: Britannica; Wikipedia; The Independent obituary (1999); Irish Times (11 September 1999); Washington Post/Reuters death notice (29 August 1999); New Catholic Encyclopedia via Encyclopedia.com

name: Isaac Lidsky
bio: An American entrepreneur, lawyer and author with an unusually varied life. A child television actor, he went on to graduate from Harvard, clerk for two justices of the United States Supreme Court, and build and sell companies, all while gradually going blind from a genetic disease. Rather than a tragedy, he came to treat his blindness as a lesson in how much of what we 'see' is really assumption and fear. In his book Eyes Wide Open and a popular TED talk, he urges readers to take responsibility for the reality they construct and to live with clear-eyed courage.
checked: Wikipedia; Harvard Law Today, 'Supreme Foresight: Isaac Lidsky 04'; TED speaker page for the TEDSummit 2016 talk; publisher record for Eyes Wide Open (Penguin Random House, 2017)

name: Ivan Nuru
bio: A young American poet, born Ivan Logan, who began writing as a teenager in Mississippi and later studied literature in New York. Drawing on his own heartbreak and the work of emotional healing, he shares spare, tender poems and prose about love, loss and self-worth, first with a large online following and then in the Amazon best-seller Offering My Heart. His brief, comforting lines, offering hope to anyone wounded in love, circulate widely on social media and quotation sites. Still early in his career, he is one of a generation of poets who found their first readers on the internet.
notes: No birth year is on record; the only indication is his own undated Goodreads author profile, which calls him a 21-year-old poet from Mississippi. Sources place him in Mississippi without naming a town, so the state is as precise as the birthplace gets. Pen name of Ivan Logan; Offering My Heart was self-published in October 2017 while he was studying literature at The New School.
checked: Her Campus interview, 'Interview with Ivan Nuru, New School Student and Published Poet'; Offering My Heart (CreateSpace, 1 October 2017) listing; his Goodreads author page

name: J. A. K. Thomson
bio: A Scottish classical scholar, born at Stonehaven on the Kincardineshire coast, who held the chair of classical literature at King's College London from 1923 to 1945. A protege and then a close friend of Gilbert Murray, he wrote on Homer in Studies in the Odyssey, traced the history of irony from Socrates onward, and examined the classical inheritance of English poetry and prose. He is remembered today chiefly for his clear, graceful rendering of Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics, published in 1953 and carried by Penguin Classics from 1955, which introduced generations of general readers to that foundational work of moral philosophy.
notes: Identity and dates now settled: James Alexander Kerr Thomson, 1879-1959, per the National Archives name authority and the Library of Congress heading. Born at Stonehaven, Kincardineshire, per the biographical sketch in British Classics outside England (2009), p. 250. Where he died is still not recorded in anything traced, so deathplace stays empty. His life is better documented than the earlier bio allowed: that sketch, and his 1908-57 correspondence with Gilbert Murray in the Bodleian.
checked: National Archives (Discovery) name authority F51340; Library of Congress / Online Books Page authority heading; British Classics outside England (2009), p. 250, via Internet Archive full-text search; Vroma, life of Grace Macurdy; Routledge author note to Irony: An Historical Introduction; Allen & Unwin 1953 and Penguin Classics 1955 editions of the Ethics

name: Jack Kerouac
bio: An American novelist and poet, the restless heart of the Beat Generation. The son of French-Canadian immigrants in a Massachusetts mill town, he crisscrossed America and dreamed of a new, spontaneous kind of writing. His novel On the Road, said to have been typed in a feverish burst onto a long roll of paper, captured a postwar hunger for freedom, movement and experience and became the movement's defining book. He wrote many others, among them The Dharma Bums, exploring Buddhism, jazz and the road. Fame sat badly on him, and he drank himself to death at forty-seven.
checked: Wikipedia; National Park Service, Lowell National Historical Park; UPI obituary in the Los Angeles Times, 22 October 1969

name: Jack Kornfield
bio: An American writer and meditation teacher who helped move Buddhist practice into the mainstream of Western life. Trained as a Buddhist monk in the forest monasteries of Thailand, Burma and India, he returned to the United States, took a doctorate in clinical psychology, and became a founder of the Insight Meditation Society in Massachusetts and Spirit Rock in California. In warm, story-filled books such as A Path with Heart he presents the path of mindfulness and lovingkindness in plain, secular language, weaving it together with Western psychology and stressing compassion, forgiveness and acceptance of a difficult heart.
notes: Born on the Marine base at Camp Lejeune, where his father was training for the invasion of Japan, not in Pennsylvania; the family moved to Philadelphia within the year, which is the likely source of the error. His own account in Lion's Roar and his twin brother Irving's self-written 2017 obituary agree on date and place.
checked: Lion's Roar, 'Meet a Teacher: Jack Kornfield' (his own account); Irving Kornfield obituary, Bangor Daily News, April 2017; Wikipedia; jackkornfield.com biography; Dartmouth Alumni Magazine (Jan/Feb 2008)

name: Jan Gehl
bio: A Danish architect and urban designer who has spent his career studying how public space shapes human life. Reacting against the car-centred planning of the 1960s, he began patiently observing, and counting, how people actually walk, sit and linger in streets and squares. His books, among them Life Between Buildings and Cities for People, argue that cities should be built at eye level and at a human pace, for walking, cycling and lingering rather than driving. Through his Copenhagen practice he has helped remake that city and advised New York, London, Melbourne and many others toward a more liveable design.
checked: Wikipedia; gehlpeople.com biography; Key Thinkers on Cities (Sage), chapter on Jan Gehl; Danish Architecture Center profile

name: Jane Jacobs
bio: An American-Canadian writer and activist who overturned the way we think about cities. With no formal training in planning, she looked hard at how real neighbourhoods work and, in her landmark 1961 book The Death and Life of Great American Cities, attacked the postwar fashion for highways, tower blocks and slum clearance. She argued that dense, mixed, walkable streets with 'eyes on the street' are what make cities safe and alive. A fierce local organiser, she helped stop expressways that would have gutted New York and Toronto, and her ideas now shape urban thinking worldwide.
checked: The Canadian Encyclopedia; Wikipedia; Los Angeles Times obituary, 26 April 2006; Project for Public Spaces profile

name: Janis Joplin
bio: An American singer whose raw, wrenching voice made her one of the defining performers of the 1960s. A misfit from a conservative Texas oil town, she found her place in the San Francisco counterculture, fronting the band Big Brother and the Holding Company and then going solo. Drawing on the blues singers she idolised, she sang with a fierce, aching intensity that seemed to hold nothing back, electrifying audiences at Monterey and Woodstock. Her hard-living, hard-drinking persona masked deep insecurity, and she died of a heroin overdose at twenty-seven.
checked: Handbook of Texas (Texas State Historical Association), 'Joplin, Janis Lyn'; Wikipedia; Los Angeles Times, Room 105 retrospective (2020)

name: Jason Fried
bio: An American entrepreneur and author, co-founder and chief executive of 37signals, the software company behind Basecamp. With David Heinemeier Hansson he wrote Rework (2010), Remote (2013) and It Doesn't Have to Be Crazy at Work (2018), books that argue for small teams, calm working hours and fewer meetings.
checked: Written from general reference knowledge on 2026-09-29 without access to sources; to be verified.

name: Jean de la Bruyère
bio: A French essayist and moralist, author of one of the classics of French prose. A quiet bachelor scholar attached as a tutor to a great aristocratic household, he watched the court and city of Louis XIV's France with a sharp, disenchanted eye. His single book, The Characters, expands an ancient model into a gallery of crisp portraits and maxims that skewer the vanity, snobbery and hypocrisy of every social type, from courtiers to the newly rich. Admired for its polished, epigrammatic style, it made him famous and won him, against opposition, a seat in the Academie francaise.
checked: Britannica; Academie francaise, notice for fauteuil 36; New Catholic Encyclopedia and Encyclopedia of World Biography via Encyclopedia.com; Wikipedia

name: Jean-Paul Sartre
bio: A French philosopher, novelist and playwright, the most famous face of existentialism. From a small, book-lined childhood he became the dominant intellectual of postwar France, holding that human beings are 'condemned to be free', thrown into a world without given meaning and wholly responsible for what they make of themselves. He set this out in the dense treatise Being and Nothingness and dramatised it in novels such as Nausea and plays like No Exit. A tireless political activist of the radical left and lifelong companion of Simone de Beauvoir, he declined the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1964.
checked: Nobel Prize in Literature 1964 facts and biographical pages (NobelPrize.org); Wikipedia; Nobel Foundation record of the declined prize

name: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
bio: The towering figure of German literature and one of the last true universal men. Born in Frankfurt, he won sudden European fame at twenty-five with the novel The Sorrows of Young Werther, then settled at the small court of Weimar, where he served as a minister of state, directed the theatre and pursued science, writing on plants, colour and anatomy. Across sixty years he produced lyric poetry, novels and above all the drama Faust, his life's work, whose restless hero bargains with the devil for boundless experience. Friend and rival of Schiller, he shaped both Romanticism and Weimar Classicism and remains Germany's national poet.
checked: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy (Goethe); Wikipedia; Goethe Yearbook article on the 1784 intermaxillary-bone discovery

name: John Archibald Wheeler
bio: An American theoretical physicist who bridged the founders of modern physics and its later generations. A collaborator of Niels Bohr, he worked on nuclear fission and the atomic and hydrogen bomb projects, then did pioneering work on gravitation and Einstein's general relativity, reviving the field. A gifted phrase-maker, he popularised the term 'black hole' and coined 'wormhole', and taught a long line of eminent physicists. In his later years he pondered deep questions linking information, observation and the very existence of the universe.
notes: Died at his home in Hightstown, New Jersey, not at Princeton, where he had taught; the deathplace had drifted to the university town. He popularised rather than coined 'black hole', and coined 'wormhole'.
checked: New York Times obituary 14 April 2008; Princeton University news release 14 April 2008; Physics World obituary (Kenneth Ford, 2008); Wikipedia

name: John Cleese
bio: A British comedian, actor and writer, one of the founders of Monty Python. Tall, precise and gifted at portraying rage and pomposity, he helped create the surreal television comedy Monty Python's Flying Circus and its films, then co-wrote and starred in Fawlty Towers, one of the most cherished of all British sitcoms, playing the manic seaside hotelier Basil Fawlty. Beyond comedy he has written and lectured on creativity, arguing that play and an unhurried, open mode of mind are essential to it. He remains a sharp, contrarian public voice into his eighties.
checked: Wikipedia; Encyclopedia.com (Contemporary Theatre, Film and Television); transcript of the 'Creativity in Management' lecture, London, 23 January 1991 (Speakola)

name: John De Paola
bio: A name attached to a handful of short motivational sayings that circulate widely online, among them the counsel to slow down so that whatever you are chasing can come around and catch you. Beyond these quotations, no reliable biography can be found: who he was, when and where he lived, and even the source of the lines are not on record, so an attribution under his name should be treated with caution.
notes: No reliable record; known only from a few circulating quotations.
checked: Internet Archive full-text search: 20 printings, all self-help, detox and gift anthologies from the 1990s on, two of them printing the line as 'attributed to'; web search returns only unrelated namesakes (the illustrator Tomie dePaola, a Florida trumpeter); no library authority record or obituary exists

name: John Dewey
bio: An American philosopher, psychologist and educational reformer, one of the most influential thinkers his country has produced. A leading figure of pragmatism, he held that ideas are tools for solving real problems and that truth is what works in practice. He is best known for transforming education, arguing that children learn by doing and by experience rather than by rote, and that schools are nurseries of democracy. Through his laboratory school and a stream of books he shaped 'progressive education' around the world, and wrote widely on democracy, art and logic.
checked: Britannica; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry on Dewey; Wikipedia; EBSCO biographical record

name: John Dryden
bio: An English poet, playwright and critic who dominated the literary life of Restoration England, so much so that the age is sometimes called the Age of Dryden. Named the first official Poet Laureate, he wrote satirical verse such as Absalom and Achitophel, odes, plays and influential translations of Virgil and other classics. His clear, vigorous, balanced style helped set the course of English poetry and prose for the century that followed, and his essays effectively founded modern English literary criticism.
checked: Britannica; Academy of American Poets biography (letters patent of 1668, first official laureate); Wikipedia. Dates are New Style; Old Style gives 9 August 1631 and 1 May 1700

name: John Lubbock
bio: An English banker, politician and scientist, a striking example of the Victorian polymath. A neighbour and friend of Charles Darwin, he was an early champion of evolution and a pioneering student of insects and of prehistory, coining the terms Palaeolithic and Neolithic. In Parliament he secured the first bank holidays and laws to protect ancient monuments, and he wrote popular books on nature and on living well. Ennobled as Lord Avebury, he embodied an age that saw no barrier between science, business and public service.
checked: Britannica (John Lubbock, 1st Baron Avebury); NatWest Group heritage biography; Royal Society Notes and Records (2014) on Pre-historic Times and the coining of Palaeolithic and Neolithic

name: John Muir
bio: A Scottish-American naturalist, writer and wilderness advocate, often called the father of the national parks. Emigrating as a boy to Wisconsin, he became a tireless walker and observer of the wild, above all of California's Sierra Nevada and the Yosemite Valley, which he described with rapturous devotion. Through vivid books and articles he taught Americans to see mountains and forests as sacred rather than mere resources, and he helped persuade the government to protect Yosemite and other wild lands. He co-founded and led the Sierra Club.
checked: Britannica; Sierra Club biography and 'A Brief Biography'; Wikipedia (death at California Hospital, Los Angeles)

name: Jon Kabat-Zinn
bio: An American scientist who brought Buddhist meditation into mainstream medicine. Trained as a molecular biologist, and a longtime student of Zen and yoga, he founded a stress-reduction clinic at the University of Massachusetts in 1979 and there developed Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction, an eight-week programme that strips mindfulness of religious trappings and teaches it as a practical skill for coping with pain, illness and stress. Backed by a growing body of research, his approach has spread into hospitals, schools and workplaces around the world.
checked: jonkabat-zinn.com biography; Wikipedia; MBSR Collaborative history of MBSR; TIME interview 'Mind Reading'

name: Jonathan Franzen
bio: An American novelist and essayist, one of the most prominent literary chroniclers of contemporary family and social life. Raised in suburban Missouri, he came to wide fame with The Corrections, a sprawling tragicomedy of a Midwestern family gathering for one last Christmas, published just days before the September 11 attacks. Freedom and Crossroads carried on his study of marriage, generation and moral striving in an anxious America. Known too for combative essays on fiction, technology and the natural world, and for a public tangle with Oprah's Book Club, he writes deliberately against the distractions of the digital age.
checked: Wikipedia; Illinois Center for the Book author record; EBSCO research starter; contemporary accounts of the September 2001 Oprah's Book Club selection

name: Jonathan Raban
bio: A British writer who became one of the most admired travel writers and essayists of his time. Trained as an academic, he left teaching to write, and made his name with literate, reflective books built around journeys: the length of the Mississippi in a borrowed sixteen-foot motorboat in Old Glory, and alone under sail around the coast of Britain in Coasting. Blending travel, memoir, history and sharp social observation, he emigrated to the United States in 1990 and settled in Seattle, writing with an outsider's clear eye about his adopted country, not least in Bad Land, on the abandoned homesteads of eastern Montana. He also wrote novels and criticism over a long and honoured career.
notes: Born at Hempton, the village adjoining Fakenham: Wikipedia and the Telegraph obituary both give Hempton, while the Guardian, New York Times and Seattle Times say only Norfolk. The Mississippi voyage of Old Glory was made in a borrowed sixteen-foot aluminium motorboat with an outboard engine, not under sail; the sailing books are Coasting and Passage to Juneau.
checked: Telegraph, Guardian, New York Times and Seattle Times obituaries, January 2023; Wikipedia; contemporary reviews and reports on Old Glory (New York Times 6 September 1981, Christian Science Monitor 9 November 1981, UPI 1 November 1981)

name: Joseph Joubert
bio: A French moralist and essayist who published not a single line in his lifetime. Secretary for a time to Diderot as a young man in Paris, and later the close friend and candid mentor of Chateaubriand, he spent his days reading, thinking and refining short reflections in the notebooks he kept from 1786 on, forever polishing thoughts on morals, art, religion and language toward a perfect concision. At his death his widow gave the papers to Chateaubriand, who in 1838, fourteen years later, printed a small private selection as 'Recueil des pensées de M. Joubert'; fuller editions of the Pensées followed through the century. He is now valued as one of the finest of French aphorists, a writer who made of hesitation and endless revision an art of its own.
notes: The bio said 'only decades after his death': Chateaubriand's selection appeared in 1838, fourteen years after Joubert died, in a small printing not put on sale. Joubert was Diderot's secretary for a few months rather than his friend on equal terms. Birth given as 6 May (Britannica, English Wikipedia) or 7 May 1754; death as 3 May (Britannica) or 4 May 1824 (French Wikipedia, booksellers' records).
checked: Britannica; English and French Wikipedia; antiquarian descriptions of the 1838 Le Normant first edition (Camille Sourget, Hatchuel) citing Escoffier and the BnF Joubert exhibition catalogue of 1954; Sainte-Beuve, Portraits littéraires

name: Joseph Roux
bio: A French Catholic priest, poet and philologist of the Limousin, in south-central France. Twelve years as curate of the mountain village of Saint-Sylvain, and afterwards of Saint-Hilaire-Peyroux, gave him a solitary life of reading and reflection, and made him a scholar and champion of his regional Occitan tongue: a majoral of the Félibrige, author of a Limousin grammar and of the epic Chansou lemouzina, and founder of the review Lemouzi. His book of aphorisms Pensées, published in Paris at the urging of the félibre Paul Mariéton, won praise from Renan and the Parisian critics, the Académie française's Prix Montyon in 1886 and a canonry at Tulle the same year; in Isabel Hapgood's English version, 'Meditations of a Parish Priest', his brief thoughts on faith, nature, solitude and character reached a wider readership still.
notes: Born at Tulle on 19 April 1834 and died in the same city in February 1905; the recorded places replace 'Limousin' and 'France', which were his region and his country. Sources differ on the day of death, 4 February (Annales du Midi notice of 1905, Occitanica) or 6 February (French and German Wikipedia); 1886, sometimes given as the death year, is the year of Hapgood's English translation. The bio's claim that he was little known in his own day is wrong: the Pensées made him famous in France and abroad, and sources date their first Lemerre edition to 1883 or 1885.
checked: René Lavaud, 'Chanoine Joseph Roux (1834-1905)', Annales du Midi 17/67 (1905), via Persée; Vidas/Occitanica biography; French and German Wikipedia; Robert Joudoux in Bulletin de l'Association Guillaume Budé (1969), via Persée; Hapgood's 1886 translation (Internet Archive, Online Books Page)

name: Joyce Brothers
bio: An American psychologist who became one of the first celebrity purveyors of popular psychology. She came to fame in an unlikely way, winning a television quiz show as an expert on boxing, then parlayed that into a long career dispensing advice on love, marriage and everyday problems through television, radio and a widely syndicated newspaper column. Warm, unflappable and ever-present in American media for decades, she helped make the insights of psychology familiar to ordinary people and became a genuine household name.
notes: Died at her home in Fort Lee, New Jersey, where she had lived for much of her adult life; the Associated Press first reported New York City and corrected it. Born in Brooklyn as Joyce Diane Bauer.
checked: New York Times obituary 13 May 2013; Washington Post obituary 13 May 2013; Fort Lee Patch report carrying the AP correction; American Psychologist obituary (Farley, 2014) via Psychology's Feminist Voices; Wikipedia

name: Jón Kalman Stefánsson
bio: An Icelandic novelist and poet, one of the most acclaimed writers of his generation in Iceland. He worked in fish factories, as a mason and as a librarian before devoting himself to literature, and his lyrical, melancholy fiction is steeped in the harsh beauty of the Icelandic landscape and the lives of fishermen and villagers. A trilogy beginning with Heaven and Hell, following a boy in a remote fishing community around 1900, won him international readers, and his novels have been widely translated, longlisted for the International Booker Prize and nominated several times for the Nordic Council Literature Prize. His prose is prized for its poetry and its feeling for solitude and loss.

name: Kamand Kojouri
bio: A contemporary Iranian poet who writes in English on love, unity and the spiritual longing of the human heart. Born in Tehran and raised in Toronto and Dubai, she settled in Britain, took an MA in creative writing in London and a doctorate at Swansea University, and later taught English and creative writing in the Gulf. Her first collection, The Eternal Dance: Love Poetry and Prose, appeared in 2018 and was followed by God, Does Humanity Exist?, which turns from romantic love to resistance and hope. Warm and idealistic, her verse circulates very widely on social media, in a tradition of devotional love poetry that reaches back to the Persian mystics.
notes: Birth year not firmly on record; the specific line quoted in the bank is unverified.
checked: Publisher-supplied author biographies (Audible, Amazon author page); author interview, Boots, Shoes & Fashion, 2020 (Tehran birth, Toronto and Dubai upbringing); Medium author profile (Swansea PhD)

name: Karolyn James
bio: A prolific writer of popular romance and romantic suspense, published almost entirely as e-books in the United States, also under the pen names London Casey and, for westerns, Claire Charlins. Her rock-star series Brothers of Rock, which follows the fictional band Chasing Cross, sold in large numbers, and its first book, All Access, reached the New York Times and USA Today lists as part of a multi-author boxed set; as London Casey she wrote the long-running Back Down Devil MC biker romances. Lines from her novels, on desire, passion and love's spark catching fire, circulate on quotation sites, though almost nothing of her life is publicly recorded.
notes: Birthplace and nationality nowhere documented, so the earlier 'USA' is removed; she is on record only as an author publishing e-books in the United States. Also publishes as London Casey and Claire Charlins, her own promotional copy naming each as a pen name of the others. The best-seller billing comes from All Access appearing in a multi-author boxed set. The exact source of the quoted line is unverified.

name: Katherine Mansfield
bio: A New Zealand-born writer who became one of the great modernist masters of the short story. She left colonial Wellington as a young woman for London, where she led an unconventional, bohemian life among writers, including a close and competitive friendship with Virginia Woolf. In spare, delicate, psychologically acute stories such as those in Bliss and The Garden Party, she caught fleeting moods and moments of revelation with a poet's precision, helping to reshape what the short story could do. Dogged by illness, she died of tuberculosis at only thirty-four.
notes: She died at Gurdjieff's Institute for the Harmonious Development of Man at Avon, immediately outside Fontainebleau, and is buried in the cemetery at Avon; sources give the death place as either Fontainebleau or Avon.

name: Kathryn Lasky
bio: An American author of books for children and young people, prolific across fiction and nonfiction. Born in Indianapolis, she has written more than a hundred books over a long career, ranging from picture books and biographies to historical novels and fantasy. She is best known for the fantasy series Guardians of Ga'Hoole, about a civilization of owls, which was adapted into an animated film, and for acclaimed historical fiction that brings the past alive for young readers. Her work has earned a Newbery Honor among other awards.

name: Keshavan Nair
bio: An Indian-born writer and management consultant who spent his career in the United States, best known for a study of the example of Mahatma Gandhi. Trained in engineering and in decision and risk analysis, and a lifelong reader of Gandhi, he taught at Ohio State University and at the Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur before a long career in consulting, rising to executive vice-president and director of Woodward-Clyde Consultants and then, from 1983, running his own practice advising senior executives on leadership. In A Higher Standard of Leadership he drew lessons from Gandhi's life for the modern workplace, arguing that leaders should be guided by absolute values, service and moral courage rather than expediency. He had earlier published Beyond Winning, a handbook on values-based leadership.
notes: Born 1932 and died 2002 on library authority records and his publisher's author note; the earlier 'dates and origin not on record' was wrong. Berrett-Koehler's jacket copy spells the birthplace 'Patalia', taken here as Patiala in Punjab. Place of death not recorded.

name: Kevin Lynch
bio: An American urban planner and scholar who transformed how we understand the experience of cities. A professor at MIT, he asked ordinary people to draw their cities from memory, and from these studies wrote his classic The Image of the City, which argued that we navigate by mental images built from five elements: paths, edges, districts, nodes and landmarks. A city that is 'legible', easy to read and remember, he held, is more usable and more humane. His ideas about how people perceive and find their way through the built environment remain foundational.

name: Kinky Friedman
bio: An American singer-songwriter, novelist, humorist and sometime politician, a proudly outrageous Texan original. He first won notice fronting the satirical country band Kinky Friedman and the Texas Jewboys, whose provocative songs mixed comedy and social commentary. He then turned to writing a popular series of comic detective novels featuring a version of himself, and to cigars, journalism and a self-mocking run for governor of Texas. Sardonic, quotable and unclassifiable, he cultivated the persona of a wisecracking cowboy philosopher.
notes: Born Richard Friedman.

name: Kurt Tucholsky
bio: A German journalist, satirist and writer of the Weimar Republic. He wrote for Die Weltbühne under his own name and as Peter Panter, Theobald Tiger, Ignaz Wrobel and Kaspar Hauser, attacking militarism, nationalism and the courts. His books include Rheinsberg (1912) and Schloss Gripsholm (1931). His works were burned by the Nazis in 1933; he lived in exile in Sweden and died in Gothenburg in 1935.

name: Kurt Vonnegut
bio: An American novelist who fused science fiction, black comedy and humane despair into some of the most beloved American books of the twentieth century. As a young soldier he survived the Allied firebombing of Dresden as a prisoner of war, an experience at the heart of his masterpiece Slaughterhouse-Five, an anti-war novel narrated with the weary shrug 'so it goes'. Across books such as Cat's Cradle and Breakfast of Champions he wrote plainly and jokingly about war, technology, free will and human folly, hiding deep pessimism and deeper kindness behind a deadpan wit.

name: L. Frank Baum
bio: An American author who created one of his country's great modern fairy tales. Born in upstate New York, he tried chicken breeding, acting, shopkeeping and journalism before finding his calling writing for children. The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, published in 1900, gave America a homegrown wonderland of a Kansas girl, a scarecrow, a tin man and a cowardly lion, and its huge success drew him on to write thirteen further Oz books. He set out to modernise the fairy tale, keeping the wonder while dropping the old moralising and terror, and his Oz has never since been out of print or out of the culture.

name: Lady Bird Johnson
bio: An American First Lady, businesswoman and conservationist, born Claudia Alta Taylor and nicknamed 'Lady Bird' as a child. A shrewd manager who built a broadcasting fortune that funded her husband Lyndon Johnson's political rise, she brought quiet strength to the White House. As First Lady she made the 'beautification' of the country her cause, campaigning to plant wildflowers and trees and to curb the billboards and junkyards blighting America's roadsides, work that helped seed the modern environmental movement. In later life she founded a wildflower research centre in Texas.

name: Lao Tzu
bio: The semi-legendary founder of Taoism and reputed author of the Tao Te Ching, the terse and paradoxical classic of the Way. Chinese tradition makes him an older contemporary of Confucius, a keeper of archives at the Zhou court who, wearied by its decline, rode west and, at a mountain pass, set down five thousand characters of wisdom before vanishing from history. Modern scholars doubt he was a single person and read the book as a compilation. Whoever shaped it, the Tao Te Ching praises yielding over force and simplicity over striving, and teaches wu wei, action so aligned with nature that it seems like doing nothing at all.
notes: Semi-legendary; some traditions place him in the 4th c. BC. Death unrecorded.
checked: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (Laozi); Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy (Laozi); Encyclopedia.com (Laozi); Wikipedia (Laozi) - all on Sima Qian's Shiji 63 account: native of Chu, keeper of the Zhou archives, senior contemporary of Confucius, five thousand characters given to Yin Xi at the pass, and the alternative fourth-century dating

name: Lee Mildon
bio: A name that survives as a newspaper byline. Short comic epigrams credited to 'Lee Mildon, Salinas (Calif.) Monterey County News' were picked up as filler by American papers in the mid-1960s, among them the line about old clothes and a big smile that later spread through quotation anthologies and greeting cards. Nothing else is recorded: no book, obituary or biographical entry has been traced, and whether the credit names a staff writer, a columnist or a reader who sent the lines in is unknown, as are dates, birthplace and everything else of the life.
notes: Not wholly unrecorded, as the row previously said: quips credited to Lee Mildon of the Monterey County News, Salinas, California, appear in The Boone-Blowing Rock Journal (N.C.), 5 March 1965, and The State Port Pilot (Southport, N.C.), 31 March 1965, the latter carrying the 'old clothes' line itself and predating every anthology printing found. Dates, places and identity still not on record.

name: Lena Horne
bio: An American singer, actress and civil-rights activist. She began as a teenage dancer at Harlem's Cotton Club and rose to become one of the first African-American performers signed to a major Hollywood studio, though the films of the era largely confined her to standalone musical numbers that could be cut for Southern audiences. name: Leonardo da Vinci
bio: An Italian polymath of the High Renaissance, the very archetype of the universal genius. The illegitimate son of a notary near Florence, he trained as a painter and produced some of the most famous images ever made, the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper, though he finished few works. But painting was only part of his restless curiosity: his thousands of notebook pages, written in mirror script, teem with studies of anatomy, water, birds, machines and the play of light, anticipating discoveries and inventions by centuries. He spent his final years in France.

bio: An American motivational speaker, author and broadcaster who rose from hard beginnings to become one of the best-known figures in his field. Born in poverty in Miami, one of twins given up for adoption, and once labelled 'educable mentally retarded' at school, he worked as a disc jockey and served in the Ohio legislature before turning to full-time speaking. name: Lewis Mumford
bio: An American historian, sociologist and critic who wrote sweepingly about cities, technology and civilization. Largely self-educated and astonishingly wide-ranging, he was for decades a leading critic of architecture and a public intellectual, warning against the dehumanising drift of the modern city and the machine. In major works such as Technics and Civilization and The City in History he traced how tools and urban forms have shaped human life, praising human-scaled community and condemning sprawl, the automobile and what he called the 'megamachine' of centralised power.

bio: An American comedian and actress, celebrated for a gallery of vivid comic characters and a long, versatile career. She rose to fame on the television show Laugh-In at the end of the 1960s with characters such as the sardonic telephone operator Ernestine, then moved between stand-up, hit films and the stage. The one-woman show The Search for Signs of Intelligent Life in the Universe, written for her by Jane Wagner, her partner of four decades and later her wife, won her a Tony Award. Sharp, warm and socially conscious, she has kept working into her eighties, one of the great comic performers of her generation.

name: Lin Yutang
bio: A Chinese writer, linguist and translator who interpreted China and the art of living to Western readers with grace and wit. The son of a Christian minister, and educated in Shanghai, at Harvard and at Leipzig, he wrote in both Chinese and English and became, for a mid-century American audience, one of the most beloved explainers of Chinese culture. His best-selling The Importance of Living made a gentle philosophy out of leisure, tea, friendship and the enjoyment of everyday things, and My Country and My People introduced Chinese life and thought to the world. He also designed the MingKwai Chinese typewriter, patented in 1952 but never manufactured, which turned typing Chinese into a matter of search and retrieval.

name: Lincoln Steffens
bio: An American journalist, one of the crusading reporters of the Progressive era whom Theodore Roosevelt dubbed 'muckrakers'. As a magazine editor and writer he exposed the machine politics and graft that ran America's cities, gathering his investigations into the influential book The Shame of the Cities. Restless and idealistic, he later grew disillusioned with piecemeal reform, and after travelling to Soviet Russia in 1919 with an American mission he reported that he had been over into the future, and it worked, a judgement that time would sour.

bio: A Brazilian singer, songwriter, actress and television presenter, and a fierce artistic voice for transgender and Black Brazilians. Born on the poor eastern edge of Sao Paulo and raised a Jehovah's Witness in the interior of the state, a faith she left as she came out, she returned to the city and took the stage name da Quebrada, 'from the hood'. Her funk and pop, confrontational and sensual by turns, put questions of gender, race, religion and desire at the centre, as on the albums Pajuba and Trava Linguas. name: Ludwig Wittgenstein
bio: An Austrian-British philosopher, among the most influential of the twentieth century. Born into one of the richest families of imperial Vienna, he gave away his inherited fortune and led a restless, self-punishing life, working as a schoolteacher, gardener and hospital porter between spells at Cambridge. He remade the philosophy of language twice over. The early Tractatus held that the limits of one's language are the limits of one's world, and that much of philosophy is nonsense, the result of trying to say what can only be shown; the later Philosophical Investigations, published after his death, undid that picture, treating meaning as a matter of use in the 'language games' of ordinary life.
