bio: A Brazilian metalworker and union leader who became one of his country's most consequential politicians. Born into deep poverty in the drought-stricken northeast and with little schooling, he lost a finger in a factory press and rose through the labour movement, leading historic strikes against the military dictatorship and helping found the left-wing Workers' Party. Elected president in 2002, he governed for two terms marked by rapid growth and vast anti-poverty programmes that lifted millions. Jailed on corruption charges later annulled by the courts, he staged a remarkable comeback, returning to the presidency in 2023.

bio: The leader of India's struggle for independence and the modern world's foremost apostle of nonviolence. Trained as a lawyer in London, he first forged his method of satyagraha, or truth-force, fighting discrimination against Indians in South Africa. Returning home, he turned the independence movement into a mass campaign of civil disobedience, spinning his own cloth, marching to the sea to make salt in defiance of British law, and fasting to still communal violence. Revered as Mahatma, 'great soul', he lived in deliberate simplicity. Months after independence and partition, he was shot dead by a Hindu extremist.

name: Majd al-Din Baghdadi
bio: A Persian Sufi master and physician of Khwarazm, in Central Asia, at the turn of the thirteenth century. Born into a wealthy family with close ties to the ruling house, he followed his father into medicine and royal service before submitting to the great mystic Najm al-Din Kubra, who set him to cleaning the latrines of his lodge to cure him of the pride of high birth. He became one of Kubra's foremost deputies and the teacher of Najm al-Din Razi, and left an Arabic treatise answering ten questions of the mystical path, along with Persian letters, poems and a treatise on spiritual travel. The Khwarazm-shah had him put to death, by tradition drowned in the Oxus, and contemporaries read the Mongol destruction of Khwarazm that followed as retribution for it.

The drowning in the Oxus is the account Sufi tradition favours, fulfilling a curse of Kubra's, while some chronicles have him cut down in his prayer room.

name: Manfred Hinrich
bio: A German philosopher, teacher, journalist and writer, and above all a prolific aphorist. Trained in philosophy and musicology, he taught in Brandenburg, worked for years as a freelance journalist and wrote children's songs, but is best known for the thousands of short sayings he called his 'Scherben', or shards. Terse, playful and often paradoxical, these aphorisms circulate very widely in German, frequently cut loose from any source, and their sheer number has made his one of the most quoted names in the genre, even where the origin of a single line is hard to trace.

name: Manuel Puig
bio: An Argentine novelist who brought the textures of popular culture into serious literature. Enthralled from childhood by the Hollywood films that lit up his dusty provincial town, he built novels out of movie fantasies, boleros, gossip and the voices of ordinary people, often dispensing with a narrator entirely. His best-known book, Kiss of the Spider Woman, in which two cellmates, a gay window-dresser and a Marxist revolutionary, pass the time retelling films, became a celebrated play and film. Openly gay and often at odds with authority, he spent much of his life in exile.

name: Marcel Proust
bio: A French novelist whose vast single work reshaped the modern novel. The sickly, sociable son of a prominent doctor, he moved for years through fashionable Parisian salons before withdrawing, asthmatic and nocturnal, into a cork-lined bedroom to write. There he produced In Search of Lost Time, a seven-volume novel of some three thousand pages in which the taste of a madeleine dipped in tea unlocks a flood of involuntary memory. Across it he anatomises love, jealousy, art, class and the workings of time and recollection with unmatched psychological subtlety. He was still revising it when he died.

name: Marcus Aurelius
bio: Roman emperor from 161 to 180 and the last of the so-called five good emperors, remembered as the philosopher on the throne. Adopted into the imperial family and schooled in Stoicism, he ruled through plague, floods and near-constant war on the northern frontier. In camp at night he wrote, in Greek and for no eyes but his own, the private notebook now called the Meditations: terse reminders to do his duty, master his temper, accept what he could not change, and remember that all things pass. Never meant for publication, it endures as one of the great works of Stoic philosophy.

bio: An American cultural anthropologist who became one of the most famous scientists of her century. As a young woman she did fieldwork in Samoa and New Guinea, and her book Coming of Age in Samoa, arguing that adolescence and gender roles are shaped far more by culture than by biology, became a best-seller. For decades she wrote, lectured and spoke out on child-rearing, women's roles, the environment and social change, bringing anthropology to a broad public. Though some of her early conclusions were later disputed, she remained a powerful liberal voice.

A restless young man who worked as a printer and a Mississippi riverboat pilot before prospecting and turning to journalism, he took his pen name from a riverman's cry for safe water. His humour, tall tales and travel writing made him famous, but his lasting glory is a pair of boyhood novels set on the great river, The Adventures of Tom Sawyer and Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, the latter a landmark for its vernacular voice and its moral reckoning with slavery.

name: Martial
bio: The Roman master of the epigram, the short, sharp, often obscene poem with a sting in its tail. Born at Bilbilis in Roman Spain, he spent much of his life in Rome as a client of the rich, and turned that dependent, sharply observant existence into twelve books of epigrams that photograph the city: its poseurs, misers, doctors, dinner parties, bores and hypocrites. Witty, indecent and humane by turns, he perfected the form, and the epigram has meant what he made of it ever since. Weary of Rome at last, he returned to Spain, where a patron's gift let him live out his days in the countryside he had missed.

name: Martin Heidegger
bio: A German philosopher whose difficult, revolutionary work reoriented much of twentieth-century thought. In Being and Time he reopened the ancient question of the meaning of being, analysing human existence as 'being-there', thrown into the world, caring, anxious and running always toward death. His later thought turned to language, technology and poetry as the places where being discloses itself. Deeply influential on existentialism, hermeneutics and later philosophy, his legacy is inseparable from the Nazi party: he joined in May 1933, took the rectorship of Freiburg as an enthusiastic supporter of the new regime, and remained a member until it fell in 1945, a stain that still troubles his readers.

Raised in Texas and trained in journalism at Austin, she went to New York in 1937, rose to managing editor of Good Housekeeping and later of McCall's, and became a senior editor at Doubleday, where she worked on the memoirs of Lyndon and Lady Bird Johnson. She wrote well over two hundred romantic stories for the women's magazines, a number of them under this name, among them 'All the Love in the World' of June 1961, the story that wedding and marriage anthologies name as the home of the widely reprinted sentence about love and time.

name: Max De Pree
bio: An American businessman and writer who became an influential voice on humane, servant leadership. He joined Herman Miller in 1947, the Michigan furniture company his father had bought and renamed in 1923 after his own father-in-law, and was its chief executive from 1980 to 1987, helping make a firm already celebrated for modern design a model of employee participation and profit-sharing. In his brief, much-admired book Leadership Is an Art, he argued that the first responsibility of a leader is to define reality and the last to say thank you, and that leadership is more a matter of stewardship, relationships and gratitude than of power. His writing remains a touchstone in management thinking.

bio: An American self-help author whose work brought the idea of codependency to a wide public. It sold millions of copies and became a cornerstone of the recovery movement. In further books and daily meditation guides such as The Language of Letting Go, she wrote with hard-won compassion about surrender, gratitude and healing.

bio: An Australian novelist who won a huge international readership with intelligent thrillers about faith, power and moral conscience. bio: An Albanian-Indian Catholic nun who became the world's most famous symbol of charity toward the poor. name: Musonius Rufus
bio: A Roman Stoic philosopher of the first century, sometimes called 'the Roman Socrates' and the teacher of Epictetus. An Etruscan of equestrian rank, he taught at Rome so pointedly that he was banished more than once by emperors wary of philosophers, on one occasion to a barren Aegean island. He left no writings; his lectures survive as notes taken down by students. Practical and humane, he argued that philosophy belongs not in the study but in daily conduct, that women as well as men should be trained in it, that marriage is a partnership of equals, and that plain food, simple dress and hard work are the ground of a good life.
notes: Dates approximate: born at Volsinii about AD 20-30, and dead by AD 101, when Pliny writes of his son-in-law Artemidorus. name: Rachel Carson
bio: An American marine biologist and writer whose work launched the modern environmental movement. Trained as a scientist and for years a writer and editor for the federal fisheries service, she first won a wide readership with lyrical books about the sea, such as The Sea Around Us. Then, alarmed by the unchecked spraying of synthetic pesticides, she wrote Silent Spring, which documented the damage that DDT and similar chemicals were doing to birds, wildlife and ultimately people. Published in 1970, its message of self-transcendence and following one's dreams made it an enormous best-seller of the era. He returned to similar themes of flight, love and the spirit in later books such as Illusions.

name: Richard Needham
bio: A Canadian newspaper columnist, long a beloved and eccentric fixture of The Globe and Mail in Toronto. Born in Gibraltar to a British army officer and brought up in India, Ireland and England, he came to Canada at sixteen, worked as a farmhand and was a reporter while still a teenager; after the Calgary Herald he joined the Globe, wrote its editorials for a few years and was then given a column of his own. It was whimsical and aphoristic, full of paradox, mischief and affection for the young, the rebellious and the underdog, and set against pomposity and authority. Needham's Inferno, one of several collections drawn from it, won the Leacock Medal for Humour in 1967.

Chief editorial writer at The Globe and Mail from 1960 to 1964 and a columnist after that, retiring in 1977. name: Richard Sennett
bio: An American sociologist who has written with unusual literary grace about work, cities and public life. Based for much of his career in New York and London, he has explored how modern society shapes character and community. In The Fall of Public Man he traced the retreat of people from a shared public realm into private life; in The Craftsman he made a wide-ranging case for the dignity and intelligence of skilled making, of doing a job well for its own sake. Across many books he writes about labour, cooperation and the built environment with a humane, critical eye.

name: Rita Mae Brown
bio: An American writer and social activist, a pioneering voice in lesbian fiction. Born in Pennsylvania, adopted as an infant and raised in York and then in Fort Lauderdale, she was active in the feminist and gay-rights movements of the 1970s and made her name with the semi-autobiographical novel Rubyfruit Jungle, a frank, funny coming-of-age story about a poor girl who is unashamedly lesbian, which became an underground classic. A versatile and prolific author, she has written poetry, screenplays, memoir and a long-running series of cosy mysteries co-credited to her cat. Witty and outspoken, she has remained a distinctive figure in American letters.

name: Robert H. Schuller
bio: An American televangelist and preacher who brought a gospel of positive thinking to a mass audience. A minister of the Reformed Church, he began preaching from the roof of a drive-in cinema in California and built a huge congregation, housed in the gleaming glass Crystal Cathedral. His television programme Hour of Power became one of the most watched religious broadcasts in the world. Influenced by Norman Vincent Peale, he preached an upbeat 'possibility thinking', teaching that faith and a positive attitude could overcome any obstacle.

name: Robert Louis Stevenson
bio: A Scottish novelist, poet and travel writer whose adventure stories have never lost their hold on readers. Trained reluctantly for the law and dogged all his life by lung disease, he travelled in search of health and material, and turned his journeys and his gift for suspense into enduring classics: the pirate adventure Treasure Island, the historical romance Kidnapped, and the dark psychological fable Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde. He also wrote tender children's verse and vivid essays. Seeking a kinder climate, he settled at last in Samoa, where he died young.

name: Robertson Davies
bio: A Canadian novelist, playwright, critic and man of letters, one of his country's most distinguished writers. He worked as an actor, a newspaper editor and the founding master of a college at the University of Toronto before winning international fame with his fiction. Written in a rich, erudite, storytelling style shot through with wit, magic and a fascination with myth and psychology, his novels come in trilogies, of which the Deptford Trilogy, beginning with Fifth Business, is the most admired. name: Robin Chase
bio: An American transportation entrepreneur and a pioneer of the sharing economy. The daughter of a US diplomat, she spent her childhood moving around the Middle East and Africa, read French, English and philosophy at Wellesley and took an MBA at MIT, and in 2000 co-founded Zipcar with Antje Danielson, the car-sharing company that let city dwellers rent a nearby vehicle by the hour and helped show that access could matter more than ownership. Buzzcar, GoLoco, the vehicle-network company Veniam and the nonprofit alliance NUMO followed, and in Peers Inc she set out her case for platforms that pool what is otherwise idle. A prominent voice on cities, climate and technology, she argues that sharing underused assets can make economies more efficient, equitable and green.

name: Robin Sharma
bio: A Canadian writer and speaker on leadership and personal mastery, one of the best-selling self-help authors in the world. Born to an Indian family in Uganda and brought to Canada as an infant, he grew up in Nova Scotia, read biology and then took a master's degree in law at Dalhousie, and worked as a litigation lawyer before self-publishing MegaLiving and then The Monk Who Sold His Ferrari, a fable about a burned-out lawyer who trades his wealth for wisdom from Himalayan sages; its success let him leave the law for good. His brisk, aphoristic advice on habits and success reaches a vast global audience.

name: Roger Mills
bio: An American psychologist, a co-founder of the approach known as Health Realization, later called the Three Principles or Sustainable Change. Trained at Princeton and then in community psychology at Michigan, he directed one of the first federally funded community mental-health programmes, in Eugene, Oregon, before developing with George Pransky an approach drawn from the teaching of Sydney Banks: that people's experience and behaviour flow from their thinking in the moment, and that helping them see this can transform lives and communities. His project in the Modello and Homestead Gardens housing developments in Dade County, Florida, brought the work national attention, and in 2004 he co-founded the nonprofit Center for Sustainable Change with his daughter. He wrote Realizing Mental Health and taught at several American universities.

name: Ron Padgett
bio: An American poet linked with the second generation of the New York School, known for plainspoken, funny and quietly moving verse. Born in Tulsa, Oklahoma, the son of a bootlegger, he moved to New York, studied at Columbia, and spent a formative year in Paris translating French poets such as Apollinaire and Reverdy, a lifelong pursuit. Over many collections his work grew clearer and more meditative, alert to the comedy and mystery of ordinary days. He reached a wide new audience when seven of his poems appeared in Jim Jarmusch's film Paterson, about a bus-driving poet, crowning a long and quietly influential career. He lives in New York City.

name: Rumi
bio: A Persian poet and Sufi mystic, today among the most widely read poets in the world. Born in the eastern Islamic world, at Balkh or nearby Wakhsh, he came west with his family as a boy, in the years before the Mongol armies reached Khorasan, and settled at Konya in Anatolia, becoming a respected preacher and teacher. His life was transformed by the wandering dervish Shams of Tabriz, whose companionship, and sudden mysterious loss, unlocked a torrent of ecstatic verse on longing and the love of God. The vast Masnavi and the Divan of Shams pour out that vision, and the whirling dance of the Mevlevi order he inspired still enacts it.

bio: An Indian-born Canadian poet and illustrator who became the face of a new, social-media-driven poetry. Her self-published first collection, milk and honey, went on to sell millions of copies worldwide, and the sun and her flowers followed. Writing without capital letters and in plain, direct language about love, trauma, womanhood, migration and healing, she has been both hugely popular and dismissed by some critics, while drawing a vast new audience to poetry.

Revered by devotees as a living god and dismissed by critics as a showman, he taught a simple ethic of love, service and the unity of all religions. bio: A British-Indian-American novelist, one of the most celebrated and most persecuted writers of his time. His fourth novel, The Satanic Verses, was condemned as blasphemous by some Muslims, and in 1989 Iran's supreme leader issued a fatwa calling for his death, forcing him into years of hiding under armed guard. He kept writing throughout, and survived a near-fatal stabbing in 2022.

name: Seneca
bio: A Roman Stoic philosopher, statesman and tragedian, born at Cordoba in Roman Spain. He rose at Rome as an orator and writer, was exiled to Corsica by the emperor Claudius, then recalled to tutor the young Nero and, for a time, to help govern the empire as his chief adviser. His moral essays and Letters to Lucilius made Stoic ethics practical and humane, urging calm before fortune and careful use of one's time, while his blood-soaked tragedies shaped later European drama. Accused at last of joining a plot against Nero, he was ordered to take his own life, and met death with the composure he had preached.

name: Sigmund Freud
bio: An Austrian neurologist who founded psychoanalysis and, more than anyone, gave the modern world its idea of the unconscious mind. Working in Vienna, he came to believe that much of mental life is hidden from us, driven by repressed desires reaching back into childhood, that surface in dreams, slips of the tongue and neurotic symptoms. Out of Josef Breuer's cathartic 'talking cure' he made the method of free association, and he mapped the mind into id, ego and superego. Fiercely controversial, he reshaped psychology, medicine and art, and left a mark on everyday language, before the Anschluss drove him from Vienna to London in 1938, a little over a year before his death.
notes: The phrase 'talking cure' was coined by Bertha Pappenheim, the patient Breuer treated as 'Anna O.'; Freud credited her with it in his 1909 Clark lectures and adopted it for psychoanalysis, while free association was his own development. He left Vienna on 4 June 1938 and died in London on 23 September 1939, so the flight came fifteen months before his death, not in his last year.

Tested: the founding of psychoanalysis, the credit for the talking cure and for free association, the id-ego-superego model, and the date of the flight from Vienna against the date of death. Two claims failed: Freud did not develop the talking cure, which was Breuer's treatment and his patient's phrase, and he did not flee in his last year.

name: Simone Weil
bio: A French philosopher, mystic and political activist of rare integrity. Brilliant and ascetic from youth, she taught philosophy while sharing the lot of those she wrote for, taking leave to labour in factories and, briefly, to join the fight in the Spanish Civil War. Her thought fused a rigorous concern for justice and human affliction with a late, unorthodox Christian mysticism of attention, self-emptying and grace. Refusing to eat more than her compatriots under German occupation, she died in England at thirty-four; almost all her work, including Gravity and Grace, appeared only after her death.

name: Socrates
bio: A Greek philosopher of Athens, regarded as a founder of Western moral philosophy. He wrote nothing; his thought is known through the dialogues of his pupil Plato and the writings of Xenophon. He questioned fellow citizens in public about justice, virtue and knowledge, a practice later called the Socratic method. In 399 BC an Athenian court convicted him of impiety and of corrupting the young, and he was executed by drinking hemlock.

name: Sogyal Rinpoche
bio: A Tibetan Buddhist teacher who became widely known in the West, above all as the author of The Tibetan Book of Living and Dying. Born in eastern Tibet and recognised as the incarnation of the visionary master Tertön Sogyal, he came to Britain in 1971 as a visiting scholar at Trinity College, Cambridge, where he took no degree, and founded the international Rigpa network of Buddhist centres; through his best-selling book he introduced many Western readers to Tibetan teachings on meditation, compassion, death and the states between lives. He retired in 2017 after senior students accused him of sexual, physical and emotional abuse, and an investigation commissioned by Rigpa upheld the accusations the following year; he died in 2019 with his legacy in dispute.

Bio corrected on two claims a Wikipedia infobox would not show: he was admitted to Trinity College, Cambridge in 1971 as a visiting scholar in theology and religious studies and never graduated, so 'educated at Cambridge' overstated it; and the abuse was not left at the level of allegation, the independent investigation by Lewis Silkin commissioned by Rigpa upheld it in August 2018.

name: Sophocles
bio: One of the three great tragic playwrights of ancient Athens, and the most honoured in his own day. A respected citizen who held public office and even served as a general, he wrote some hundred and twenty plays and won the city's dramatic festival again and again across a long life. Only seven survive complete, among them the towering Theban plays Oedipus the King and Antigone, which probe fate, pride, justice and the limits of human knowledge. He is credited with adding a third actor to the stage and deepening the art of character, and his Oedipus became for Aristotle the very model of tragedy.
checked: Britannica (123 dramas, seven surviving, the third speaking actor and painted scenery, the generalship with Pericles in the Samian War); Encyclopedia.com (Hellenotamias in 443/442, general 441-439, membership of the Athenian senate); Wm. Blake Tyrrell, 'The Suda's Life of Sophocles', Electronic Antiquity 9.1, which treats the treasurership of 443/442 and the eighteen victories at the City Dionysia as the two securely documented facts of his life; Wikipedia for the 30 competitions, 24 wins and never lower than second, and for Aristotle's use of Oedipus Rex in the Poetics. Tested: the count of plays, the repeated festival victories, the public office and generalship, the hedged credit for the third actor, and Aristotle's judgement of Oedipus.

name: Stanisław Lem
bio: A Polish writer of science fiction and philosophy, the most widely read in the genre outside the English language. Trained in medicine and steeped in science, he used the form to explore the limits of human knowledge and the near-impossibility of truly grasping the alien or the future. His novel Solaris, filmed three times, imagines a living planet-ocean that defeats every human attempt to understand it. Elsewhere, in satirical fables and mock reviews of nonexistent books, he wrote with dazzling wit about robots, technology and the follies of reason, foreseeing much of the digital age.
notes: Solaris has been filmed three times, not twice: a 1968 Soviet television film by Boris Nirenburg and Lidiya Ishimbayeva, Tarkovsky's 1972 film and Soderbergh's 2002 film. Only the last two were made for the cinema, which is what the earlier count of two reflected. Lem finished medical studies at the Jagiellonian University but deliberately sat no final examinations, taking only the absolutorium, so he was trained in medicine without holding a medical degree.
checked: Wikipedia's Lem article (Theodore Sturgeon's 1976 judgement that he was the most widely read science fiction writer in the world; translation into more than 40 languages and 45 million copies; medical studies at Lwow and the Jagiellonian with final examinations refused to avoid service as a military doctor; the 1968, 1972 and 2002 Solaris films); Wikipedia's 'Solaris (1968 film)', which calls the Soviet television version the first adaptation of the novel; BFI feature 'Before Tarkovsky: the little-known original version of Solaris'. Tested: the reach claim, the medical training and whether a degree was implied, the number of Solaris adaptations, the planet-ocean description, and A Perfect Vacuum as the reviews of books that do not exist. One claim failed: the novel has been filmed three times.

name: Steve Jobs
bio: The American entrepreneur who co-founded Apple and did more than anyone to shape the look and feel of modern digital life. Adopted and raised in what became Silicon Valley, he started Apple in a garage with Steve Wozniak and helped bring the personal computer to ordinary people. Forced out of his own company, he built the computer firm NeXT and turned Pixar into an animation powerhouse before returning to a near-bankrupt Apple and leading one of the great corporate revivals with the iMac, iPod, iPhone and iPad. A demanding perfectionist obsessed with design and simplicity, he died of cancer at fifty-six.

name: Sylvia Plath
bio: An American poet and novelist whose intense, unflinching work made her one of the defining voices of confessional poetry. Brilliant and driven from childhood, she wrote poems of ferocious imagery and emotional extremity, collected above all in the posthumous Ariel, and a single autobiographical novel, The Bell Jar, about a young woman's breakdown. Her turbulent marriage to the poet Ted Hughes and her lifelong struggle with depression shadow the work. She took her own life in London at thirty, and was later awarded a posthumous Pulitzer Prize, her reputation still growing.
checked: The Pulitzer Prizes official list for 1982 (Poetry: The Collected Poems, Harper & Row); Britannica on The Collected Poems, edited by Hughes, published 1981, awarded the 1982 prize; Wikipedia (The Bell Jar published a month before her death under the name Victoria Lucas, Ariel 1965, death in London 11 February 1963 aged 30). Tested: the confessional-poetry standing, Ariel as the posthumous collection, The Bell Jar as her only novel and its subject, the marriage to Hughes, the age at death, and the posthumous Pulitzer.

name: T.C. Boyle
bio: An American novelist and short-story writer known for exuberant language, dark comedy and a restless range of subjects. Born Thomas John Boyle in New York's Hudson Valley, he adopted the middle name Coraghessan as a young man and trained at the Iowa Writers' Workshop. Over some twenty novels and more than a hundred and fifty stories he has written about ecology and obsession, immigration, communes, and historical cranks and visionaries, in books such as The Tortilla Curtain and The Road to Wellville. Prolific and stylistically dazzling, he founded the undergraduate writing program at the University of Southern California and taught there for close to forty years.
notes: Publishes as T. C. Boyle; full name T. Coraghessan Boyle.
checked: tcboyle.com author page (MFA from the Iowa Writers' Workshop 1974, PhD in nineteenth-century British literature from Iowa 1977, in the USC English department since 1978); Wikipedia (born Thomas John Boyle Jr., middle name changed to Coraghessan at seventeen, 'more than 150 short stories'); Encyclopedia.com's Contemporary Authors entry; his 2019 Kenyon Collegian interview, in which he says he founded the undergraduate writing programme at USC and has stepped down from the professorship; Westchester Magazine, April 2026 ('twenty novels'), and the Writers on Writing interview recorded 27 March 2026 for the novel No Way Home, which confirm he is living and still publishing. Tested: the birth name and the adopted middle name, the Iowa training, the subjects and titles named, the teaching post, the counts of novels and stories, and whether he is alive. One claim failed: 'hundreds of stories' overstates a body of some hundred and fifty; the novels, at twenty, were understated as 'more than a dozen', and the teaching is now specified and dated.

name: T.S. Eliot
bio: An American-born British poet, critic and playwright, one of the towering figures of literary modernism. Born in St. Louis and educated at Harvard, he settled in England, worked as a banker and then a publisher, and eventually became a British subject and a devout Anglican. His early poems, above all The Waste Land, a fragmented, allusive vision of a spiritually barren modern world, revolutionised English poetry, while his later Four Quartets turned toward faith and time. A hugely influential critic and the author of verse dramas, he won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1948.

S. Eliot Foundation's own pages 'T. S. Eliot at Lloyds Bank' and '100 years since T. S. Eliot entered the world of publishing' (clerk from 19 March 1917, resignation November 1925, editor and director at Faber and Gwyer); nobelprize.org for the 1948 Literature prize. Tested: the American birth and British subjecthood, the Harvard education, the bank-then-publisher career, the Anglican conversion, The Waste Land and Four Quartets, the verse dramas, and the Nobel year.

name: The School of Life
bio: Not a person but an organisation, an educational company opened in a disused stationery shop in Bloomsbury, London, in September 2008 by the curator Sophie Howarth and the philosopher Alain de Botton. Through books, films, online courses, classes and a range of products, it sets out to teach 'emotional intelligence', the skills of self-knowledge, relationships, calm, work and living wisely that conventional schooling tends to leave out. Drawing on philosophy, psychology and culture, and known for its calm, accessible online videos watched by many millions, it has become a widely recognised popular voice in the modern wellbeing and self-understanding movement.
notes: An organisation founded by two people, not an individual author. Founder credit corrected: the row gave the founding to Alain de Botton with unnamed 'colleagues', but the co-founder was Sophie Howarth, and the contemporary record puts her first. NPR in September 2008 and Time in November 2008 both call Howarth the school's founder and director and describe de Botton as a faculty member; Howarth's own site says 'I was the co-founder, with Alain de Botton, of The School of Life'.

name: Theodore Roosevelt
bio: The twenty-sixth president of the United States, a whirlwind of energy who embodied the vigorous 'strenuous life' he preached. A sickly, asthmatic boy who remade himself through exercise and will, he was by turns a rancher, historian, naturalist, soldier and reformer before becoming, at forty-two, the youngest president in the nation's history. In office he broke up monopolies, protected vast tracts of wilderness as national parks and forests, and set the digging of the Panama Canal under way, winning the Nobel Peace Prize for mediating an end to the Russo-Japanese War. Out of office he hunted in Africa and mapped an unknown river in the Amazon, and he remains an enduring American icon.
notes: The exploring came after the presidency, not before it: the Smithsonian-Roosevelt African expedition of 1909-10 and the Roosevelt-Rondon descent of the River of Doubt in 1913-14. Construction of the Panama Canal was secured and begun in his term, from 1904, but the canal opened in 1914, five years after he left office.
checked: Britannica ('a writer, naturalist, and soldier'; the 1906 Nobel Peace Prize for mediating an end to the Russo-Japanese War; 'secured the route and began construction of the Panama Canal (1904-14)'; the two years ranching in Dakota Territory from 1884); Wikipedia (boyhood asthma and the strenuous life, The Naval War of 1812 as the making of his reputation as historian, police and Navy posts, Rough Riders, governor, then the four-month Amazon expedition after the 1912 defeat); Miller Center 'Life Before the Presidency'; Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library on the 1913-14 Brazilian expedition. Tested: each pre-presidential role in the list, the age of forty-two and the youngest-president claim, the trust-busting, the conservation record, the canal, and the Nobel. Two claims failed: he was no explorer before 1901, that career belonging to 1909-14, and the canal he began in office was finished five years after it.

name: Thomas Brasch
bio: A German writer, poet, playwright and filmmaker of a rebellious, restless spirit. Born in English exile to Jewish Communist émigrés, a father from Berlin and a mother from Vienna, who settled in the Soviet zone of Germany after the war to help build the socialist state, he grew up a privileged but dissident son of that state, was jailed for handing out leaflets against the crushing of the Prague Spring, and left for the West in 1976. There he won acclaim for poetry, prose, plays and films marked by anger, irony and linguistic energy. Caught between two Germanys and at home in neither, he became a distinctive voice of the divided nation.
notes: Bio corrected: the parents were not both German. His father, Horst Brasch (1922-1989), was a Berlin Jew who reached Britain on a Kindertransport in 1939 and did return; his mother, Gerda Wenger (1921-1975), was a Viennese Jew who escaped to Britain in 1938 on a domestic-servant visa, married Horst in London in 1944 and had never lived in Germany, so 'German-Jewish parents who returned' was wrong twice over. Dates and place confirmed: born 19 February 1945 at Westow, Yorkshire, died of heart failure in Berlin on 3 November 2001, aged 56. Sources differ on the family's move, Suhrkamp giving 1946 and filmportal and de.wikipedia 1947. In 1968 he was sentenced to 27 months for leaflets against the invasion of Czechoslovakia, denounced by his own father, and released on probation the next year; the exit permit came in December 1976.
checked: Suhrkamp author page and the publisher's printed Zeittafel for Brasch (born 19 February 1945 at Westow, Yorkshire, to Jewish emigrants; 27-month sentence in 1968 for 'staatsfeindliche Hetze'; exit permitted December 1976); filmportal.de biography (father Horst state secretary and deputy culture minister, mother Gerda a journalist, father's denunciation in 1968); de.wikipedia Horst Brasch, citing the Vienna Jewish community birth register of 1921 via JewishGen for Gerda Wenger, 'die gebürtige Wienerin', married in London in 1944; NDR feature of 19 February 2025 (died 3 November 2001 aged 56 of heart failure)

name: Thomas Carlyle
bio: A Scottish historian, essayist and social critic, one of the most powerful and combative voices of the Victorian age. From humble beginnings in rural Scotland he became a prophetic man of letters in London, writing in a dense, thunderous, idiosyncratic prose all his own. His vivid history The French Revolution made his name, and in works such as Sartor Resartus and On Heroes he attacked the materialism and mechanisation of the age and preached the importance of great men, work and moral earnestness. His authoritarian later politics have since dimmed his reputation.
checked: Britannica (Scottish historian and essayist, Ecclefechan 1795 to London 1881, move to Cheyne Row in 1834, The French Revolution begun there); Encyclopedia.com and the Victorian Web biography, both of which date the making of his name to the three volumes of The French Revolution in 1837, after Sartor Resartus had appeared in Fraser's in 1833-34 and been damned by the press; Wikipedia for On Heroes (1841), Past and Present (1843) and the hardening of the later politics. Tested: the nationality and the rural origins, the London career, the attribution of his reputation to The French Revolution, the titles named, the anti-mechanist and great-man themes, and the dimming of his standing. No conflict with the ledger, which traces the line once given to Buddha to his 1829 essay 'Voltaire'.

name: Thomas Gray
bio: An English poet and scholar, one of the most admired poets of the eighteenth century though he wrote very little. A retiring, melancholy man who spent most of his life as a scholar at Cambridge, he perfected a small body of exquisitely crafted verse. His Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard, a grave, tender meditation on death, obscurity and the unfulfilled lives of the rural poor, is one of the best-known and best-loved poems in the English language. He declined the post of Poet Laureate, preferring his quiet, studious retirement.
checked: Thomas Gray Archive biography and its record of letters 258-259, where the laureateship vacated by Cibber's death on 12 December 1757 is offered through William Mason on behalf of the Duke of Devonshire and declined, Whitehead being appointed on 19 December; Gray's own letter of 19 December 1757 ('I would rather be Serjeant-Trumpeter, or Pin-Maker to the Palace'), also printed in the University of Otago laureate exhibition; Wikipedia (fellow of Peterhouse then Pembroke, only thirteen poems published in his lifetime, the Elegy of 1751). Tested: the smallness of the output against the reputation, the Cambridge scholar's life, the description of the Elegy, and above all the refusal of the laureateship, which holds in the primary correspondence.

name: Thomas Robert Dewar (Lord Dewar)
deathplace: Homestall, near East Grinstead, Sussex, England
bio: A Scottish whisky magnate, businessman and celebrated wit. With his brother he built the family firm John Dewar and Sons into a global whisky empire, pioneering flamboyant advertising and travelling the world to promote Scotch. Made a peer as Baron Dewar, he was a famous sportsman, racehorse owner and after-dinner speaker, and his sharp, epigrammatic sayings, sometimes called 'Dewarisms', circulated widely, among them the line long attributed to him that a mind is like a parachute, working only when it is open. He is remembered for those quips as much as for his whisky.
notes: Deathplace corrected from London: he died at his country house Homestall, near East Grinstead in Sussex, on 11 April 1930, and was cremated at Golders Green. He was long resident at the Savoy in London, which is likely the source of the error. The 'parachute' line circulated as his but he is better described as its populariser than its coiner; it is also misattributed to Frank Zappa.
checked: scotchwhisky.com 'Whisky Heroes: Tommy Dewar' by Gavin D Smith (born Perth 1864, son of the founder John Dewar; the maxims known as 'Dewarisms'; MP for St George's 1900-06; knighted 1902, baronet 1917, Baron Dewar of Homestall 1919; bred Challenger and Cameronian; died April 1930 aged 66, cremated Golders Green); Parks & Gardens record for Thomas Dewar ('died on 11 April 1930 at his Sussex home, The Homestall, East Grinstead'); History of Parliament peerages database, letters patent of 20 May 1919; Oxford DNB entry heading 'Dewar, Thomas Robert, Baron Dewar (1864-1930), whisky blender and politician'; on the parachute line, Barry Popik's citations and the English StackExchange survey of them, which find it unattributed in the Louisville Times of October 1927 and Dewar's name attached only from April 1928, i.e. populariser and not coiner, as the row already says

name: Thích Nhất Hạnh
bio: A Vietnamese Zen master, poet and peace activist who did more than almost anyone to carry mindfulness to the West. Ordained young, he founded schools and a monastic order and led a movement of 'engaged Buddhism' serving villagers caught in the Vietnam War. His call for peace led Martin Luther King to nominate him for the Nobel and cost him his country: exiled for four decades, he settled in France and founded the Plum Village community. In simple, luminous books and talks he taught awareness of the present moment in walking, breathing and washing dishes, reaching millions before returning to Vietnam to die where he was first ordained.

Tested: the young ordination, the schools and the order, the engaged-Buddhism movement, the King nomination, the length of exile, Plum Village, and the return to die at the temple where he was ordained.

name: Tom Robbins
bio: An American novelist whose exuberant, playful, wildly digressive fiction made him a hero of the counterculture. A former newspaperman who settled in the Pacific Northwest, he wrote comic, philosophical novels stuffed with outrageous metaphors, wordplay and offbeat wisdom, celebrating freedom, imagination, sex and mischief against conformity. Books such as Even Cowgirls Get the Blues, with its hitchhiking heroine, and Jitterbug Perfume won a devoted following. Prizing delight and individual liberty above all, he cultivated a sunny, mischievous outlook across a long life.
checked: New York Times, Washington Post and Seattle Times obituaries of 9-10 February 2025 (death at his home in La Conner, Washington, aged 92); Cascadia Daily News, 9 February 2025 (copy editor at the Richmond Times-Dispatch, then Seattle, 'the Hells Angel of Art Criticism'); Wikipedia (born Blowing Rock 22 July 1932, Seattle Times art critic and Post-Intelligencer copy desk, La Conner from 1970, Even Cowgirls Get the Blues 1976, Jitterbug Perfume 1984). Tested: the newspaper career, the Pacific Northwest, the counterculture standing, Sissy Hankshaw as the hitchhiking heroine, the titles, and the fact and place of his death.

name: Tony Robbins
bio: An American self-help author, coach and motivational speaker, one of the most successful and recognisable figures in the industry. Rising from a difficult, impoverished youth, he built a vast business empire around high-energy seminars, best-selling books such as Awaken the Giant Within, and the coaching of executives, athletes and even presidents. Physically imposing and relentlessly upbeat, he preaches that people can transform their lives by mastering their psychology, emotions and daily habits. Admired by a huge following and doubted by critics, he helped define the modern personal-development seminar.

The bio's 'coaching of executives, athletes and even presidents' holds up as far as the press does: the Washington Post of 11 January 1995 and Bob Woodward's The Choice place him at Camp David with the Clintons over the weekend of 30 December 1994, and a 1998 Independent profile lists Clinton, Gorbachev and Andre Agassi among his clients. Confirmed living and still touring in 2026.

Mahavorić, 29 February 1960, North Hollywood; Glendora High School; Unlimited Power 1986, Awaken the Giant Within 1991); Washington Post, 'New Age "Guru to the Glitterati" Advised Clintons', 11 January 1995, and the Washington Post excerpt from Woodward's The Choice; The Independent profile, 1998; 2026 event listings for his Leadership Academy, Fiji Life & Wealth Mastery and the Business Mastery event of 12-16 August 2026

name: Truman Capote
bio: An American writer of exceptional style whose life became as famous as his work. A precocious talent from the Deep South, he made an early mark with lyrical fiction and then with the sparkling novella Breakfast at Tiffany's. His masterpiece, In Cold Blood, a chillingly detailed account of the real murder of a Kansas family, he called a 'nonfiction novel' and helped invent a new genre. A celebrated wit and social butterfly who moved among the rich and famous, he squandered his later years in drink, drugs and feuds.

name: Tschingis Aitmatow
bio: A Kyrgyz writer, by far the best-known author to come out of Soviet Central Asia. Writing in both Kyrgyz and Russian, he drew on the folklore, landscapes and hard rural life of his homeland to create humane, lyrical stories that reached readers across the Soviet Union and beyond. His tender early tale Jamila, a story of love against tradition, made his name, and later novels such as The Day Lasts More Than a Hundred Years blended realism, legend and quiet dissent. He became a symbol of his people to the wider world.
notes: Chingiz Aitmatov (German spelling).

name: Tyler Durden
bio: A fictional character, the charismatic anarchist at the heart of the 1999 film Fight Club, adapted from Chuck Palahniuk's novel. A soap salesman and underground fight-club founder who preaches liberation from consumerism and the comforts of modern life, Durden is eventually revealed to be a projection of the unnamed narrator's own splintered mind. His swaggering exhortations to stop clinging to possessions and control, and simply let go, are widely quoted. The words belong to the character and the film's screenplay, by Jim Uhls, not to any real person.
notes: A fictional character, not a real author.
checked: AFI Catalog entry 61148 for Fight Club (1999), giving David Fincher as director, Jim Uhls as sole credited screenwriter, and 'Based on the novel Fight Club by Chuck Palahniuk (New York, 1996)', with Brad Pitt credited as Tyler Durden and Edward Norton as 'Narrator'; 20th Century Studios' own page for the film; the character is the soap salesman with whom the unnamed narrator founds the fight club, and is revealed as the narrator's projection

name: Uta Hagen
bio: A German-American actress and one of the most influential acting teachers of the twentieth century. Born in Germany and raised in the United States, she had a distinguished career on the Broadway stage, creating roles such as Martha in the original production of Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf? Blacklisted during the McCarthy era, she poured her energy into teaching at a New York studio, where she trained many leading actors. Her books Respect for Acting and A Challenge for the Actor remain standard texts of the profession.
checked: Britannica (German-born American actor; the family moved to the US when she was seven; three Tony Awards, one of them for creating Martha in Albee's Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf?); the New York Public Library finding aid to the Uta Hagen and Herbert Berghof Papers (blacklisted from television for most of the 1950s and subpoenaed by HUAC, second Tony in 1963, head of HB Studio after Berghof's death in 1990, died at home on 14 January 2004); Guardian obituary, 17 January 2004 (Respect for Acting, 1973, still a standard text in acting schools); Encyclopedia.com's Hagen entry (Berghof founded HB Studio in 1945, Hagen began teaching there in 1947 and taught until months before her death). Tested: the German birth and American upbringing, the origination of Martha in the 1962 Broadway premiere, the blacklisting, the studio and its pupils, and the two books. The bio rightly stops short of crediting her with founding HB Studio; her teaching began in 1947, before the blacklist, but the bio claims only that she poured her energy into it, which the record supports.

name: Vangisa
bio: One of the earliest named poets of the Buddhist tradition, a monk in the Buddha's own community. Remembered as a former wandering reciter drawn to the Buddha's teaching, he was praised as foremost among the disciples in spontaneous poetic inspiration. A body of verse attributed to him survives in the Pali canon, in which he celebrates his teacher, wrestles openly with pride and lust, and mourns the death of his preceptor. He is known only through these ancient scriptures, which make him at once a figure of devotion and one of the first personal voices in Indian Buddhist poetry.
notes: Ancient figure known only through Buddhist scripture; dates nominal. Also written Vangisa/Vangisa.
checked: Malalasekera's Dictionary of Pali Proper Names, entry Vangisa Thera (consulted at palikanon.com and wisdomlib): brahmin family versed in the Vedas, the skull-tapping livelihood, ordination by Nigrodhakappa, and the Buddha's declaration of him as foremost among those of ready expression, patibhanavantanam, at AN i.24, with his verses at Thag 1208-79, repeated at SN i.183ff, among them the self-admonitions against conceit at his facility of speech, the verses on desire, and the long elegy for Nigrodhakappa. John D. Ireland, Vangisa: An Early Buddhist Poet, BPS Wheel 417/418, which prints the Pali and translation of Thag 1253 / SN 8.12: kaveyyamatta vicarimha pubbe gama gamam pura puram, that is, Intoxicated with skill in the poetic art, formerly we wandered from village to village, from town to town. Then we saw the Awakened One and faith arose in us. Jonathan Walters's translation of the Vangisa-thera-apadana at SuttaCentral (the Buddha places him foremost among eloquent monks). Tested: the wandering poet before the going forth, which rests on his own verse and not only on the commentary; the foremost-in-inspiration title; the verses on pride, on lust and on his preceptor's death; and the absence of any record of him outside the canon and its commentaries. Agrees with the ledger, which gives Sn 3.3 to Vangisa and not to the Buddha.

name: Veronica A. Shoffstall
bio: An American writer remembered for a single, much-loved poem. She wrote 'After a While' as a nineteen-year-old college student in 1971, a tender meditation on growing up through heartbreak and learning self-reliance, planting one's own garden rather than waiting for someone to bring flowers. Widely reprinted, often anonymously or misattributed to Jorge Luis Borges, it became a staple of greeting cards and graduation speeches under titles she had never given it, 'Comes the Dawn' among them; when Ann Landers ran it unattributed in the 1980s, she proved and copyrighted her authorship. A graduate of SUNY Oswego who served for decades at the Bahá'í International Community's United Nations office in New York, she grew up on Long Island and spent the rest of her life in the city.
notes: Dates and birthplace corrected: her 2024 obituary and Find a Grave give born 24 September 1952 at Astoria, Queens, New York, and died in early 2024 (obituary 14 February 2024), not born 1946 with no death. She wrote 'After a While' at nineteen in 1971 while at SUNY Oswego, which fits 1952 and not 1946. Deathplace left unset: the funeral was at Ozone Park, Queens, but the exact place of death is not stated. 'Comes the Dawn' is not the poem's opening but a title it acquired in the Ann Landers column; Shoffstall wrote that she never titled the poem at all and would never have chosen that one, and registered it for copyright as 'After a While'. The words themselves close a rival version of the poem claimed by Judith B. Evans, whose last line runs 'with every good-bye comes the dawn'.
checked: Bergen Funeral Service obituary, February 2024, as carried by Legacy.com (born 24 September 1952 to Edward and Lucretia Shoffstall; McArthur High School, Levittown, 1970; a bachelor's degree from SUNY Oswego, where she wrote the poem; the Ann Landers printing in the 1980s and her proof of authorship; decades of service at the Bahá'í International Community's United Nations Office and Office of Public Information; the move into New York City after college); Shoffstall's own email, quoted at wherepoetrycrosses.blogspot.com, disowning the title ('I never titled it Comes the Dawn - that was something it picked up along the way... I call it After a While'); PolyArchive's account of the Borges misattribution, the Buenos Aires subway poster and the Ann Landers history; Bertram's Blog for the Judith Evans variant ending 'with every good-bye comes the dawn'. Tested: the age and year of composition, the degree (she did take it), the Borges misattribution, the Ann Landers episode and the copyright, the Bahá'í connection, and whether 'Comes the Dawn' is the poem's opening. One claim failed: that phrase is neither hers nor the poem's first words.

name: Vince Lombardi
bio: An American football coach regarded as one of the greatest and most quoted in the sport's history. Brought up in an Italian family in Brooklyn, the son of a butcher, he took over a struggling Green Bay Packers team and, through relentless discipline, drive and attention to fundamentals, turned it into a dynasty that won five championships in the 1960s, including the first two Super Bowls. The Super Bowl trophy now bears his name. His fierce sayings about winning, effort and commitment made him a byword for competitive determination, above all 'winning isn't everything, it's the only thing', a line he spread rather than coined: the college coach Red Sanders had used it in 1948.
notes: Not his coinage: Henry 'Red' Sanders, then of Vanderbilt, told a Birmingham quarterback club on 9 November 1948 that with the fans winning isn't everything, it's the only thing, fourteen years before the saying was first fastened on Lombardi in print, and Esquire in November 1962 quotes Lombardi with the different adage that winning isn't everything but wanting to win is. The parentage is also looser than 'the son of Italian immigrants': his father Enrico was born at Salerno in 1889 but brought to Brooklyn as a child of two, while his mother Matilda Izzo was born in New York to immigrants from Vietri di Potenza.
checked: Quote Investigator, 'Winning Isn't Everything; It's the Only Thing' (Barry Popik's citation from The Birmingham News, 9 November 1948, for Sanders; the Esquire piece of November 1962 and the LIFE profile of December 1962, the first to ascribe the pointed form to Lombardi; QI's conclusion that on current evidence Sanders crafted the expression); Wikipedia's Lombardi article (birth in Sheepshead Bay to Enrico 'Harry' Lombardi of Salerno and Brooklyn-born Matilda Izzo, the family meat business, three straight NFL championships in 1965-67 and championships in five of seven seasons, Super Bowls I and II, and the renaming of the Super Bowl trophy in 1970); Encyclopedia.com (Enrico brought from Italy in 1892 aged two; 'second-generation Italian immigrant parents'); New World Encyclopedia (Brooklyn-born mother). Tested: the parentage, the state of the Packers when he arrived, the count of championships, the trophy, and the authorship of the winning line. Two claims failed.

name: Virginia Woolf
bio: An English writer, one of the foremost modernist novelists and a central figure of the Bloomsbury Group. In novels such as Mrs Dalloway, To the Lighthouse and The Waves she pioneered a fluid 'stream of consciousness' that follows the inner life of her characters moment by moment, dissolving conventional plot. A brilliant essayist and critic, she argued in A Room of One's Own for women's creative and economic independence, a founding text of feminist criticism. Plagued throughout her life by mental illness, she drowned herself in a river in Sussex at fifty-nine.
checked: Britannica's Woolf article (best known for Mrs. Dalloway, 1925, and To the Lighthouse, 1927, with The Waves, 1931; 'pioneering essays on artistic theory, literary history, women's writing, and the politics of power'; death on 28 March 1941 'when she was 59 years old'); the Wikipedia article for the Bloomsbury Group, A Room of One's Own of 1929 and the drowning in the River Ouse near Rodmell. Tested: the Bloomsbury standing, the three novels named, A Room of One's Own as the argument for women's creative and economic independence and as a founding text of feminist criticism, the lifelong illness, and the age of fifty-nine at her death, which the dates give exactly. The bio claims 'pioneered' for the technique and not for the term 'stream of consciousness', which was William James's coinage and was first turned on fiction by May Sinclair, so it does not overreach.

name: Virginie Ancelot
bio: A French writer, playwright and painter, and the celebrated hostess of a Parisian literary salon. Born in Dijon and married to the dramatist Jacques Ancelot, she wrote successful comedies and dramas for the Paris stage, along with novels and memoirs. For decades her salon was a gathering place for the writers, artists and politicians of Restoration and July-Monarchy France, and her memoirs became a valued record of that world. A talented painter as well, she was a notable woman of letters in an age that gave women few such opportunities.
checked: Library of Congress name authority nr90000139 (born Dijon 15 March 1792, died Paris 1875), citing La Grande Encyclopédie of 1886 and Bénézit, which calls her a French portrait and genre painter; IdRef/BnF authority 029446139, ark:/12148/cb12107172f ('Peintre et femme de lettres. Auteur de nouvelles, de romans et de nombreuses pièces de théâtre'; married to the dramatist Jacques-Arsène-François-Polycarpe Ancelot, 1794-1854); CERL Thesaurus cnp01383191 (birth Dijon, death Paris 7e, with the Archives de Paris death record no. 621 registered 21 March 1875); her salon ran on the rue de Seine from 1824 to 1866, and her Salon debut as a painter was in 1814. The authority records date the death 21 March 1875 where fr.wikipedia gives 20 March; the year, which is all the row carries, is not in doubt

name: Wayne Dyer
bio: An American self-help author and speaker often called the father of modern motivation. Raised partly in Detroit foster homes and an orphanage, he took a doctorate in counselling, worked as a school guidance counsellor and taught at St John's University in New York, publishing counselling textbooks with John Vriend, before Your Erroneous Zones, an attack on guilt, worry and self-defeating habits, became one of the best-selling titles of its kind and launched a new career. Over thirty years and some forty books he moved from practical psychology toward spirituality, drawing on the Tao and on the power of intention, and became a fixture of public television, teaching that we shape our lives by the thoughts we choose.
notes: Your Erroneous Zones (1976) was his first book for a general readership, not his first book: Counseling Techniques That Work, written with John Vriend for APGA Press, is dated 1974 by the Library of Michigan's author record and 1975 by Open Library. The obituaries repeat the 'first book' shorthand, but the bibliographic record does not support it. The teaching post is also stated exactly here rather than as a professorship in general: he was an assistant, later associate, professor at St John's University from 1971.
checked: Library of Michigan Michigan Authors record for Dyer (BS 1965, MS 1966 and EdD in counselling 1970, all at Wayne State; counsellor at Pershing High School 1965-67; director of guidance at Mercy High School 1967-71; assistant professor at St John's University 1971-74; Counseling Techniques That Work with John Vriend, APGA Press, 1974; Your Erroneous Zones, Funk & Wagnalls, 1976); Open Library's author search sorted oldest first, whose earliest Dyer titles are the 1975 printings of Counseling Techniques That Work; CBS News obituary, 30 August 2015 (fans 'dubbed him the father of motivation'; the orphanage and foster homes; teaching at St John's when the book altered his course); Associated Press obituary via Legacy.com (more than 40 books; ten PBS specials that raised more than $250 million for public television; death at his Hawaii home of a heart attack). Tested: the epithet, the foster homes and orphanage, the doctorate, the teaching post and its rank, whether Your Erroneous Zones was his first book, the count of some forty books over thirty years, the turn to the Tao and to intention, and the public-television career. One claim failed.

name: William Blake
bio: An English poet, painter and printmaker, unrecognised in his own lifetime and now regarded as one of the great visionary artists in the language. A London engraver of fierce independence and religious imagination, he claimed to see visions from childhood and created his own private mythology. In illuminated books that he made entirely by hand, among them Songs of Innocence and of Experience, he fused radical poetry and startling images into a single art. Rebellious against reason, empire and orthodoxy alike, he celebrated imagination, energy and spiritual liberty.
checked: Poetry Foundation's biography of Blake ('Poet, painter, engraver, and visionary'; 'Though in his lifetime his work was largely neglected or dismissed'; the illuminated-writing method of etching text and design together on a copper plate; Songs of Innocence with its title page dated 1789, combined with the companion Songs of Experience in 1794; the Lambeth prophecies and the private mythology of Urizen and Los; Jerusalem in a hundred illuminated plates; his account of organised religion as a perversion of ancient vision). Tested: the trade of engraver and the London life, the visions claimed from childhood, the illuminated books made by hand, the titles named, the private mythology, and the neglect in his own lifetime.

name: William Bruce Cameron
bio: An American sociologist and educator. A university professor and author of textbooks introducing sociology to students, he wrote, in his 1963 book Informal Sociology, the now-famous sentence that not everything that can be counted counts, and not everything that counts can be counted, a caution about the limits of measurement in the social sciences. That line is very frequently misattributed to Albert Einstein, but scholarship has traced it firmly to Cameron. Beyond his academic work, little of his personal biography is on record, and even his dates are not reliably documented.
notes: Born year set to unknown: the 1915 birth and the widely repeated 1976 death both trace only to quote aggregators and AI-written profiles. The one Library of Congress name-authority heading 'Cameron, W. Bruce, 1960-' (n2001024987) belongs to the later novelist W. Bruce Cameron, not this sociologist. Often misattributed to Albert Einstein.
checked: Quote Investigator, 'Not Everything That Can Be Counted Counts, and Not Everything That Counts Can Be Counted', which prints the passage from Informal Sociology (Random House, 1963), page 13, checked on paper against the fifth printing, and traces one component phrase back to Cameron's article 'The Elements of Statistical Confusion Or: What Does the Mean Mean?', AAUP Bulletin 43:1, Spring 1957, verified on JSTOR; Garson O'Toole, Hemingway Didn't Say That (2017), page 406, found in the Internet Archive corpus; the Internet Archive scans of both Informal Sociology printings, whose title pages give his post as Bradley University in 1963 and the University of South Florida in the later issue; the American Sociological Association's 1955 annual meeting programme (William Bruce Cameron, Bradley University, 'Some Personal and Social Ramifications of the Jazz Aesthetic'); his Social Forces book reviews of 1967 and 1968 from the University of South Florida and a 1964 article from the University of Tampa; Modern Social Movements (Random House, 1966). Tested: the 1963 book and the wording of the sentence, the Einstein misattribution and the scholarship correcting it, and the claim that little is recorded of him. His teaching career is traceable through Bradley, Tampa and South Florida and he had worked as a professional musician, but no reference work gives his dates, so the bio and the existing note both stand.

name: William Carlos Williams
bio: An American poet and physician, a major figure of modernist poetry who found the extraordinary in ordinary American life. For more than forty years he practised as a family doctor in his home town of Rutherford, New Jersey, writing poems between patients. Rejecting the dense allusiveness of contemporaries like Eliot, he sought a fresh, plain American idiom and famously insisted on 'no ideas but in things', capturing concrete images in spare, clear lines. His long poem Paterson and his whole example deeply influenced later American poets.
checked: Encyclopedia.com's Contemporary Authors entry (born Rutherford 17 September 1883, MD from the University of Pennsylvania 1906, postgraduate paediatrics at Leipzig, practice at Rutherford from 1910, died 4 March 1963); the Annals of Thoracic Surgery profile, 'William Carlos Williams (1883-1963): physician-writer', which dates the first incapacitating stroke to 1951 and says it forced him to retire 'after 40 years of practice'; Rosenthal and Wagner-Martin's life for the Modern American Poetry site (practice opened at Rutherford in 1910, first stroke March 1951); Wikipedia (both paediatrics and general medicine, chief of paediatrics at Passaic General Hospital, 'No ideas but in things' from 'A Sort of a Song' and repeated throughout Paterson, Paterson published in five volumes 1946-58). Tested: the length of the practice, which runs 1910 to March 1951 and so is more than forty years; the town; the family-doctor description; the rejection of Eliot's manner in favour of an American idiom; the phrase 'no ideas but in things' and its place in Paterson; and the influence on later poets.

name: William James
bio: An American philosopher and psychologist, often called the father of American psychology. The brother of the novelist Henry James, he trained in medicine and then established one of the first psychology laboratories in the United States, writing the monumental Principles of Psychology. As a philosopher he was a leading champion of pragmatism, the view that the truth of an idea lies in its practical consequences, and in The Varieties of Religious Experience he examined faith with sympathy and a scientist's eye. He shaped how Americans think about mind, belief and action.
checked: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, entry on William James, whose chronology gives the birth at New York City in 1842 as the first child of Henry James senior, the birth of his brother Henry in 1843, medical school and the return to it in 1866, and '1874-5. Begins teaching psychology; establishes first American psychology laboratory', together with The Principles of Psychology (1890), the Gifford Lectures of 1901-2 published as The Varieties of Religious Experience (1902), and Pragmatism (1907). Tested: the medical training, the standing as father of American psychology, the laboratory (the bio's hedged 'one of the first' is if anything more cautious than the SEP's 'first'), the Principles, the brotherhood with the novelist, and the account of pragmatism as truth in practical consequences - a term coined by Peirce and spread by James, which the bio does not claim for him - and the Varieties.

name: William Shakespeare
bio: The most celebrated writer in the English language, a poet and playwright of unmatched range and influence. Born in the market town of Stratford-upon-Avon, he made his career in London as an actor, playwright and shareholder in a leading theatre company. In some thirty-eight plays, comedies, histories and the great tragedies Hamlet, King Lear, Macbeth and Othello, and in his sonnets, he explored the whole span of human nature with a poetic power and psychological depth that have never been equalled. His words and characters permeate the culture, and his plays are performed the world over.
checked: The Shakespeare Birthplace Trust biography (born 1564 at Stratford-upon-Avon, died 1616; a founding member of the Lord Chamberlain's Men, its regular dramatist at about two plays a year for almost twenty years, remaining as the company became the King's Men; 'Shakespeare's works include 38 plays, 2 narrative poems, 154 sonnets'; the First Folio gathered by fellow actors after his death). Tested: the count of some thirty-eight plays, the London career as actor, playwright and sharer in a leading company, the market-town birth, and the four tragedies and the sonnets named.

name: Winston Churchill
bio: A British statesman, soldier and writer, best remembered as the prime minister who led the United Kingdom through the Second World War. A descendant of dukes with a restless, pugnacious energy, he had a long and turbulent political career, and a reputation for poor judgement, before 1940, when, as war leader, his defiance and stirring oratory rallied Britain in its darkest hour against Nazi Germany. A prolific historian and journalist, he won the Nobel Prize in Literature, and his wartime speeches and quips are among the most quoted in the language.
checked: The Nobel Prize's own facts page for the Literature prize of 1953 (born 30 November 1874 at Woodstock, died 24 January 1965 in London; educated at Harrow and Sandhurst; a brief army career, then Conservative MP from 1900 and high office in Liberal and Conservative governments; First Lord of the Admiralty at the outbreak of the war, Prime Minister and Minister of Defence from May 1940 to 1945 and again 1951-55; the prize 'for his mastery of historical and biographical description as well as for brilliant oratory'; the war memoirs and the life of his ancestor the first Duke of Marlborough). Tested: the war premiership, the descent from the Marlborough dukes, the soldiering and journalism, the long and turbulent career before 1940, and that the Nobel was in Literature and not Peace.

name: Woody Guthrie
bio: An American singer-songwriter and folk musician whose songs became the voice of the Depression-era poor and a foundation of American folk music. A wandering Oklahoman driven from the Dust Bowl, he rode the rails and sang for migrant workers and union halls, writing hundreds of songs of hardship, protest and hope, most famously 'This Land Is Your Land', his tart answer to complacent patriotism. His guitar bore the slogan 'This machine kills fascists'. Struck down by a hereditary disease, he directly inspired Bob Dylan and generations of protest singers.
checked: Library of Congress, 'This Land Is Your Land' in the Patriotic Melodies collection (written February 1940 in reaction to Irving Berlin's 'God Bless America', originally titled 'God Blessed America for Me', first recorded with Cisco Houston in April 1944); the Woody Guthrie Center biography (the slogan painted on his guitar in the early 1940s and kept there after the war, Huntington's disease inherited from his mother, most of his last thirteen years in hospital, death on 3 October 1967); Wikipedia (hundreds of songs, Dust Bowl Ballads and the Dust Bowl Troubadour name, death at Creedmoor Psychiatric Center in Queens, the nineteen-year-old Bob Dylan visiting him at Greystone Park and idolising him). Tested: the answer to 'God Bless America' and its edge against complacent patriotism, the guitar slogan, the riding of the rails and the singing for migrants and unions, the hereditary disease, the place of death, and the direct influence on Dylan.

name: Zadok Rabinowitz
bio: A Hasidic rabbi and one of the most original and prolific Jewish thinkers of nineteenth-century Poland, usually known as Rabbi Zadok HaKohen of Lublin. A former Talmudic prodigy of the non-Hasidic world who came to lead a Hasidic community, he wrote voluminously and daringly across Jewish law, theology, mysticism and the philosophy of history, blending rigorous scholarship with Kabbalistic and psychological insight. His many works, published largely after his death, are still closely studied for their depth and originality.
notes: Zadok HaKohen of Lublin (Zadok Rabinowitz). Birthplace corrected from Kraslava: he was born at Krustpils, then called Kreuzburg, in the Vitebsk Governorate of the Russian Empire, now the town of Jēkabpils in Latvia. Died at Lublin.
checked: YIVO Encyclopedia of Jews in Eastern Europe, 'Tsadok ha-Kohen of Lublin' (1823-1900; born at Kreuzburg in Courland to a Latvian and Lithuanian family; a prodigy married early; follower of Mordekhai Yosef Leiner of Izhbits; inherited Leibele Eger's position at Lublin in 1888; Tsidkat ha-tsadik 1902, Dover tsedek 1911, Mahshevot haruts 1912, responsa Tif'eret Tsevi 1909); Encyclopaedia Judaica entry reproduced at Encyclopedia.com, 'Zadok ha-Kohen Rabinowitz of Lublin' (born Kreuzburg (Krustpils), Courland; the 'illui of Krinik'; refused publication in his lifetime and asked for it after his death); Seforim Blog essay by Dovid Bashevkin, 2010 (34 years of seclusion 1854-1888; died 9 Elul, Monday 3 September 1900, in his seventy-seventh year)

name: Zeno
bio: The founder of Stoicism, born at Citium on Cyprus and probably of Phoenician descent. A merchant by trade, he was shipwrecked near Athens and, browsing in a bookseller's, stumbled on philosophy; he studied with the Cynics and others before opening a school of his own. He taught in the Stoa Poikile, the 'painted porch' along the Athenian marketplace, and it is from that colonnade that Stoicism takes its name. He held that the aim of life is to live in agreement with nature and reason, that virtue alone is truly good, and that the wise stand unmoved by fortune, laying the ground for Seneca, Epictetus and Marcus Aurelius.
notes: The bank's 'Zeno' is Zeno of Citium, the Stoic.
checked: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Eminent Philosophers 7.1-4, in Yonge's translation at Fordham's Internet History Sourcebook (Citium, a Greek city partly settled by a Phoenician colony; a cargo of purple from Phoenicia and shipwreck close to the Piraeus; the bookseller's stall and the second book of Xenophon's Memorabilia; Crates pointed out to him, then Stilpo, Xenocrates and Polemo); Britannica's Zeno of Citium (Athens about 312 BC, the Cynic Crates and Stilpon of Megara, teaching in the Stoa Poikile 'whence the name of his philosophy', ethics central, happiness in conforming the will to the divine reason); Wikipedia for the contested Phoenician ancestry and for the Stoa Poikile as a colonnade in the Agora. Tested: the founding of Stoicism, the hedged 'probably of Phoenician descent', the merchant's trade and the shipwreck, the bookshop story, the Cynic teachers, the Painted Porch as the source of the school's name, and the doctrines of life in agreement with nature and of virtue as the only good.
